frame.statement: A self-reflection on PASS.md B3 and B4: for each capability interface and each cross-cutting concern, state the idealistic future state a build could reach today, tool-agnostic where a standard allows it, and ask it from several angles, because how a standard is used matters more than whether it is used. Score each answer on a closed scale that separates absent from exists from directionally aligned, and marks alignment toward something that would not work as an error.

window.means: the state of technology in the last six months; what could be developed right now

scale.label: misaligned
scale.means: Built toward something that would not work, or against where the standard is going. An error to correct, not a gap to fill.

scale.label: exists
scale.means: Something exists, but its use is nominal or its direction cannot be judged from the evidence.

scale.label: aligned
scale.means: Exists and is directionally aligned with the future state stated for the section.

scale.label: leading
scale.means: At or beyond the future state stated for the section, with the evidence to show it.

angles.asks: Is the standard or interface present at all? The single litmus test; never sufficient on its own.
Are the standard's distinguishing mechanisms in use, the ones that separate real adoption from a label?
Does the element sit behind a capability interface with a proven second adapter, so the core imports the interface and never the implementation?
Do the cross-cutting concerns ride on this element without the caller asking, and which ones apply here?
How does a caller use it across every entry (human, event, schedule, external), and how does it compose with the other elements?
Is the build aligned with where the standard and its ecosystem are heading inside the window, and what would be an error to build now?

settledness.means: The standard is the principled baseline with no credible competitor; the question is how deeply it is used.
Two or more candidates are live; the future state names the property to hold, not the winner.
The direction is visible but no standard has settled; the future state names the direction and the exit if it changes.
PASS.md records no standard; the future state is original design held to the B5 specification.

frame.isolation: The crew that writes this questionnaire reads PASS.md Part B and the web, and nothing this repo built from them. The check refuses any text that names a thing in this repo, and any product name outside the direction and settledness fields.

standard.name: OCI Runtime Spec
standard.why: The runtime specification is the only vendor-neutral contract for container configuration, lifecycle and hardware settings, and it remained active inside the window: v1.3.0 landed with 24 merged pull requests and added a vm.hwConfig object aimed at VM-based runtimes. The candidates people compare - gVisor, Kata Containers, Firecracker microVMs, WebAssembly runtimes behind the runwasi shim - are implementations selected behind that one specification, not competing specifications, so the open question is depth of use rather than which spec wins.

future_state.text: The proposed future state: a unit of work runs isolated per the runtime specification, and the isolation request is expressed only as specification-shaped configuration - root filesystem and mount set, namespace and user mapping, resource limits, network posture, and the hardware configuration where a virtual-machine class runtime serves - never as engine-specific flags. The core imports an isolation capability whose operations are create, start, wait, signal, delete, plus snapshot, pause, resume and fork where the class supports them, and at least two adapters from different isolation classes serve it, chosen by name at dispatch so a workload needing faster start, stronger boundaries or foreign hardware changes the adapter and not the core. Budget, identity, policy, telemetry and provenance attach to the sandbox lifecycle without the caller naming them, and the exact set of things allowed to cross the boundary - files in, artifacts out, credentials, network egress - is declared per unit rather than inherited from the host.

direction.text: Inside the window the isolation class for untrusted agent output settled on hardware-virtualised or syscall-intercepting sandboxes rather than shared-kernel containers, and the startup-cost argument that used to justify the weaker boundary was abandoned: cold start is now 90ms-200ms and 'the remaining gap between container and microVM speed is no longer a strong justification for weaker isolation'. The specification itself moved toward this by adding a hardware-configuration object for VM-based runtimes in v1.3.0, and multi-tenant platforms now treat gVisor, Kata Containers and Firecracker microVMs as interchangeable primitives behind one shim-shaped handle. What is settling beyond start-and-stop is machine-state lifecycle - pause, resume and server-side fork of a paused sandbox carrying memory, overlay and running processes - which is how long-running and parallel agent work is made affordable. It would be an error now to build a shared-kernel container as the security boundary for untrusted agent output, to treat isolation as a deployment concern outside the interface, or to couple the core to one hypervisor's control API so that the second adapter can only ever be a sibling of the first.
direction.quote: the remaining gap between container and microVM speed is no longer a strong justification for weaker isolation

questions.question: Proposed question: Is there a named isolation capability whose contract cites the runtime specification and a version, and does every unit of work reach execution through it?
questions.evidence_expected: The interface definition showing the specification and version it claims, plus an execution record for one unit showing it ran inside an isolated runtime.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The contract names the specification and a version, and every execution path - not only the one used for untrusted input - resolves through that interface.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Isolation is described only in deployment configuration or prose, no version is claimed, or one or more execution paths run work directly on the host.

questions.question: Proposed question: Which distinguishing fields of the runtime configuration are actually set per unit of work - read-only root filesystem, explicit mount set, user and namespace mapping, CPU, memory and process limits, network posture, and the hardware configuration where a virtual-machine class runtime serves - and where does each value come from?
questions.evidence_expected: The generated runtime configuration for one real unit, with a line-by-line account of which field came from the unit's declaration and which is a default, and the run that shows a limit being enforced.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The configuration is derived from the unit's declared needs, is restrictive by default, denies host networking and privilege unless declared, and every non-default is justified; a limit breach is observably enforced.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: The configuration is the runtime's default, or is privileged, shares the host network or mounts the host filesystem broadly; nothing distinguishes one unit's sandbox from another's.

questions.question: Proposed question: Do two adapters from genuinely different isolation classes pass the same conformance suite, and does the core import only the interface?
questions.evidence_expected: The conformance suite, a run of it against both adapters, and a dependency listing or import graph showing the core has no reference to either implementation.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The second adapter breaks a different assumption than the first - for example a hardware-virtualised boundary against a syscall-interception boundary, or a locally hosted runtime against one on hardware the build does not own - and the swap is exercised in an automated gate, not by hand.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: There is one adapter; or the second is the same class from a different vendor; or the core reaches an implementation's control API directly, so the interface is decorative.

questions.question: Proposed question: Which cross-cutting guarantees ride on the sandbox lifecycle without the caller asking - a ceiling that terminates the unit and not the platform, an actor named on every sandbox start including delegated agent actors, a policy decision taken before the sandbox boots, telemetry spanning the lifecycle, and provenance binding produced artifacts to the code version, inputs and actor?
questions.evidence_expected: A telemetry record for one sandbox lifecycle showing actor, correlation and budget attributes; a refusal captured before boot; and an artifact record naming the code version, inputs and actor that produced it.
questions.aligned_looks_like: All five are applied by the platform, are present identically for a unit no caller configured, and a ceiling breach terminates that unit alone.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Limits or attribution are optional arguments a caller may omit, refusal happens after the sandbox has already spent resources, or a sandbox can start with no named actor.

questions.question: Proposed question: How does a caller obtain isolation from each of the four entries - a human, an event, a schedule, an external system or agent - and what is declared to cross the boundary in each case?
questions.evidence_expected: One unit of work driven through all four entries with the resulting runtime configurations placed side by side, plus the declared inventory of inputs, outputs, credentials and egress for each.
questions.aligned_looks_like: One code path serves all four, the configuration is identical except for identity and budget, and what crosses the boundary is declared per unit rather than inherited from the host environment.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Interactive work runs unisolated for convenience while only externally triggered work is sandboxed, or each entry builds its own configuration, or host credentials and network are visible inside the sandbox by default.

questions.question: Proposed question: Does the build use machine-state lifecycle operations - pause, resume, and fork of a paused sandbox - where the isolation class offers them, and is it free of the errors the window has ruled out?
questions.evidence_expected: A run in which a long-running or idle unit is suspended and later resumed from saved state, or a paused sandbox is forked for parallel attempts, together with the timing and the interface signature that makes the operation optional per class.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Suspension, resumption and forking are capability operations with a defined answer when an adapter cannot serve them, and the security boundary chosen for untrusted output is not a shared kernel.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Untrusted agent output runs behind a shared-kernel boundary; or long-running work is kept alive by holding a machine idle because no suspend exists; or the core assumes one implementation's snapshot API.

gaps.claim: That the runtime specification itself defines pause, resume, snapshot or fork as standard lifecycle operations, rather than these being adapter-specific extensions.
gaps.research_query: OCI runtime specification lifecycle operations pause resume checkpoint restore standardisation status

gaps.claim: Which isolation class operators running hundreds of concurrent agent units actually default to, with measured cost per resident sandbox.
gaps.research_query: operators running hundreds of concurrent agent sandboxes 2026 default isolation class measured cost per resident sandbox

standard.name: Completions wire convention (see F-b3-03)
standard.why: The request shape is a de facto convention rather than a published specification, and inside the window at least two shapes are live at once: the message-based completion format, which its originator says will remain supported indefinitely as an industry standard, and an item-and-response format that agentic work is moving toward. A second family is served alongside it - gateways expose an Anthropic-style messages endpoint and translate to and from the OpenAI-compatible format - so a build cannot treat any single wire format as the settled one. The property to hold is that the core imports a model-access capability and never a wire format.

future_state.text: The proposed future state: the core imports a model-access capability whose operations are a completion, a streamed completion, a tool-call turn and a schema-constrained structured output, with the widely-implemented request shape as the transport convention and at least two adapters that differ in execution model - one multi-provider hosted endpoint and one engine served on hardware the build controls - so no provider name appears above the boundary. Affordances that materially change cost or behaviour are first-class fields of the interface rather than opaque passthrough: cache directives, reasoning effort, and a usage record that separates prompt, cached-prompt, reasoning and completion tokens; each is verified end to end after translation rather than assumed to have survived it. Every call carries a ceiling that terminates the unit when exceeded, a named actor, a policy decision taken before the call, and telemetry attributes recording the model actually served, the routing or fallback decision, and the per-request cost, so that a cost estimate can be produced before commitment and reconciled against what was spent.

direction.text: Inside the window the wire convention consolidated rather than fragmented - 'In 2026, OpenAI-compatible APIs have become the de facto standard' - while the shape carried over it split in two: the message-based completion format stays supported indefinitely as an industry standard, and an item-and-response format built for tool use, reasoning and multi-output turns is where agentic traffic is heading. Gateways now serve a second, Anthropic-style messages endpoint beside the first and translate between them, which is direct evidence that the durable boundary is the capability, not the format. The second thing settling is what the boundary is expected to enforce: per-request and per-session token ceilings to stop runaway agent loops, hierarchical per-team budgets, and per-request cost and token attribution. The failure mode the window documents is silent semantic loss - a failover in which a translating layer 'quietly dropped the cache directive on the floor - no error, no warning' - and under-counting cost because reasoning tokens never appear in the visible answer. It would be an error now to require callers to use a client library the build wrote, to hard-code one provider's request builder into the core, to treat a uniform wire shape as proof that provider-native directives took effect, or to bet the interface exclusively on the message-based format when agentic turns are moving to items and responses.
direction.quote: quietly dropped the cache directive on the floor - no error, no warning

questions.question: Proposed question: Is there a model-access capability with a declared request and response contract, and is every model call in the build made through it?
questions.evidence_expected: The interface definition, and a search across the executing code showing no direct provider call sites outside the adapters.
questions.aligned_looks_like: One contract, every call routed through it, and the wire convention it speaks named explicitly with the format variant it targets.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Model calls are made in several places with provider-specific code, or the contract exists but some paths bypass it.

questions.question: Proposed question: Which mechanisms beyond a plain completion are exercised and verified - streaming, tool-call turns, schema-constrained structured output, cache directives, reasoning effort, and a usage record separating prompt, cached, reasoning and completion tokens?
questions.evidence_expected: For each mechanism, a request and response pair captured at the boundary showing the directive sent and the provider-reported effect returned; and for cost, a reconciliation of the build's recorded usage against the provider-reported usage fields for the same call.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Each mechanism is exercised on both adapters, and the effect is verified from the response - a cache hit is observed, not hoped for - with reasoning tokens counted in cost.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Only plain completions are used; or directives are set in the request and never checked in the response; or cost is estimated locally from visible text, so reasoning-heavy calls are under-counted.

questions.question: Proposed question: Do two adapters with different execution models pass one conformance suite, and does the same suite catch semantic loss in translation - a directive dropped, a usage field missing - rather than only checking that a response came back?
questions.evidence_expected: The conformance suite, its results on both adapters, and at least one case in the suite that fails when a translated directive does not take effect.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The second adapter differs in execution model rather than being another catalogue of the same shape, and the suite asserts on semantics, not just on a non-empty response.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: One adapter; or a second that is a different vendor of the same hosted shape; or a suite whose assertions a translation layer could pass while silently discarding directives.

questions.question: Proposed question: Are the ceiling, the named actor, the pre-execution policy decision, the telemetry attributes and the replay-safety of a retried call applied by the platform on every model call, with no way for a caller to decline them?
questions.evidence_expected: A telemetry record for one call showing model served, routing or fallback decision, actor, correlation and cost; a refusal recorded before any spend; and evidence that a retried call did not double-charge or double-act.
questions.aligned_looks_like: A unit that exceeds its ceiling is terminated while the platform continues; a refusal is deterministic and precedes the call; every call is attributable to an actor and a correlation.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Budgets are advisory, enforced only by a downstream provider, or expressed as a caller-supplied argument; refusal happens after the tokens are spent; fallback is invisible in the record so cost cannot be attributed to the model that actually served.

questions.question: Proposed question: How does a caller make a model call from each of the four entries, what is the minimum they must supply, and how does the call compose with cost estimation before commitment?
questions.evidence_expected: The same task driven from a human entry, an event, a schedule and an external caller, with the call sites shown; plus the estimate produced before execution and the recorded actual cost for the same unit.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The caller names a capability and a task, never a provider or a model identifier, the field set is the same at all four entries, and an estimate is produced by a pure function before anything is spent and is later reconciled against the actual.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: A caller must select a provider or model, or must pass credentials, or must use a client library the build wrote; or cost is only knowable after the run.

questions.question: Proposed question: Is the interface shaped so that a move from the message-based format to an item-and-response format, or the addition of a second wire family, is an adapter change rather than a core change - and does anything in the core assume one format?
questions.evidence_expected: The interface's own type definitions, an account of which fields are format-specific, and a demonstration or a written migration path showing what a second wire family would require.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The interface speaks in turns, items and typed results of its own, adapters translate, and adding a second wire family touches only adapters and their conformance runs.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: The core's types are one provider's request and response objects renamed; or the build has bet on a single format with no stated exit; or per-provider branches sit above the boundary.

gaps.claim: That a published specification, rather than a de facto convention, now governs the completion request shape.
gaps.research_query: published open specification for LLM completion request format standards body 2026

gaps.claim: Whether hard budget termination at the model boundary is a common production practice or mostly a documented feature.
gaps.research_query: production evidence enforced token budget termination LLM gateway 2026 case studies measured

standard.name: - (no standard; see B5)
standard.why: PASS.md records no standard for this row, and research inside the window found none: the engines converge on the same primitive - 'a function that resumes exactly where it left off after a crash' - but each expresses it in its own SDK, and portability is discussed as a procurement preference against lock-in rather than as a specification anything conforms to. Temporal, Restate, DBOS and Inngest differ in whether durability lives in a dedicated cluster, in a library, or in a database already trusted for state, so the future state must be original design held to the B5 specification, not an adoption of someone else's shape.

future_state.text: The proposed future state, held to the B5 specification for the seam with no standard: one contract for a multi-step unit of work, written in the platform's own vocabulary of step, idempotency key, checkpoint and resume point, and specifying the request shape, the result shape, cancellation semantics, timeout and budget enforcement, partial-result handling, and what a failure returns as a typed object. Every non-deterministic result - a model output, a tool result, a clock reading, a retrieval - is journaled at first execution and replayed from the journal on recovery rather than re-run, and every step that touches the outside world carries an idempotency key so that at-least-once delivery becomes effectively-once effect. A restart resumes at the first incomplete step under the budget that remained, not a fresh one, and carries the same actor, correlation and provenance chain across the discontinuity. At least two executors serve the contract and differ in execution model - one with a server process, one without - and a deliberate crash mid-run is part of the definition of done, not a thought experiment.

direction.text: Inside the window durable execution moved from niche to expected for agent work, with pipelines chaining model calls, long-running sagas and event-driven jobs all 'converging on the same primitive: a function that resumes exactly where it left off after a crash'. What is settling is the mechanism set: journaled steps, replay of recorded results rather than re-execution, timers and indefinite waits that survive redeploys, and an at-least-once guarantee that leaves duplicate suppression to idempotent steps. What is being abandoned is the assumption imported from deterministic workflow code that a step can simply be re-run on recovery: agent workflows are packed with non-determinism, and a model call cannot be replayed and pretended to be the same event - its output must be recorded once and reused. What has not settled, and shows no sign of settling inside the window, is a common specification across engines; portability remains a procurement preference. It would therefore be an error now to write the platform's step contract in one engine's vocabulary, to depend on deterministic replay of model or tool calls, to let a resumed run start with a fresh budget, or to treat 'the engine gives us exactly-once' as a substitute for idempotency keys on outward actions.
direction.quote: converging on the same primitive: a function that resumes exactly where it left off after a crash

questions.question: Proposed question: Is there a written contract for a multi-step unit of work that names its own step, checkpoint and resume-point vocabulary, and does it cover all six things the specification requires - request shape, result shape, cancellation, timeout and budget enforcement, partial results, and what a failure returns?
questions.evidence_expected: The contract document or interface definition, mapped item by item against those six requirements.
questions.aligned_looks_like: All six are specified in the platform's own vocabulary, and the contract is what the executors implement rather than a description of what one of them happens to do.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: There is no contract and each execution path checkpoints in its own way; or a contract exists but leaves cancellation, partial results or failure shape undefined.

questions.question: Proposed question: How are non-deterministic results handled across a restart: is a model call, tool result, clock reading or retrieval journaled at first execution and replayed from the journal, or is it re-executed on recovery?
questions.evidence_expected: A recorded run that was killed mid-flight and resumed, with the journal showing which results were replayed and which steps re-ran, and the count of outward calls made before and after the restart.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Every non-deterministic result is recorded once and reused on recovery; the resumed run makes no duplicate outward call and produces the same intermediate values it had before the crash.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Recovery re-runs completed steps and calls the outside world twice; or the design assumes model calls are replayable; or checkpointing exists only between whole runs, so a crash loses everything since the start.

questions.question: Proposed question: Do the ceiling, the actor and delegation chain, the pre-execution refusal, the correlation attributes and the provenance chain survive a restart, and does a resumed run continue under the budget it had left?
questions.evidence_expected: A crash-and-resume run showing budget remaining before and after, the actor and correlation attributes on both sides of the discontinuity, and the provenance record linking artifacts produced after the resume to the same inputs and code version.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The resumed run continues with the remaining ceiling, the same named actor and delegation chain, and one unbroken correlation and provenance chain; exceeding the ceiling terminates that unit and nothing else.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: A resume starts with a fresh budget, loses the actor or delegation chain, opens a new correlation, or produces artifacts that cannot be tied back to the inputs of the original run.

questions.question: Proposed question: Do two executors with genuinely different execution models pass one conformance suite, and does that suite include a real crash rather than a simulated one?
questions.evidence_expected: The conformance suite, its results against both executors, and the run in which a process is killed mid-step and the unit completes correctly on resume.
questions.aligned_looks_like: One executor uses an external server process and the other has none, both pass unmodified, and the crash test is part of the automated gate; the core imports neither executor.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: One executor; or a second that is a different product of the same architecture; or a suite whose durability claim rests on an exit code with no step actually interrupted.

questions.question: Proposed question: How does a caller start, observe, cancel and resume a multi-step unit from each of the four entries, and what does an externally triggered replay of the same unit do?
questions.evidence_expected: The same multi-step unit driven from a human entry, an event, a schedule and an external caller; a cancellation issued mid-step and the result it returned; and a replayed external trigger with the effects counted.
questions.aligned_looks_like: One field set at every entry, cancellation returns a defined result rather than an exception, a replayed trigger is recognised and produces no second effect, and a schedule-driven run is indistinguishable downstream from a human-driven one.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Cancellation is best-effort with an undefined result, a replayed external trigger runs the work again, or one entry has its own bespoke start path.

questions.question: Proposed question: Is the contract written in vocabulary the build owns rather than in the vocabulary of whichever engine is installed, and is there a stated exit if that engine is replaced?
questions.evidence_expected: The contract's type names and error names set beside the installed executor's API, plus the written migration path and the evidence that the second executor was built against the contract and not against the first executor's shape.
questions.aligned_looks_like: No engine-specific concept - worker registration, task queue names, replay determinism rules - appears in the contract; the exit is written down and demonstrated by the second executor.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: The contract is one engine's SDK with the names changed; or the interface requires deterministic replayable code, which forecloses executors that journal instead; or there is no stated exit because the engine is assumed permanent.

gaps.claim: That any cross-engine specification or portable journal format for durable execution exists or is being drafted inside the window.
gaps.research_query: cross-engine durable execution specification portable workflow journal format working group 2026

gaps.claim: What resumption latency and journal size production users of many long-running agent workflows actually observe.
gaps.research_query: production measurements durable agent workflow resume latency journal size 2026 postmortem

standard.name: Agent Client Protocol
standard.why: For the editor-to-agent seam the protocol is at a stable version 1 with SDKs in five languages, adoption by JetBrains, Google and GitHub and 25+ agents, and dozens of implementations as of August 2026 - so the direction is clearly visible. It has not settled for the case this platform needs most, a headless server-side turn: the protocol's permission and client-facing mechanics assume an interactive client, non-interactive runs need a permission profile that can proceed headlessly, and a second host-side protocol (Microsoft's Agent Host Protocol) appeared in the window at an adjacent layer. Governance is consolidating - MCP, A2A and ACP now sit under Linux Foundation stewardship with the same sponsors backing several - which points to layering rather than one winner, so the future state names the direction and the exit.

future_state.text: The proposed future state: the unit of agent execution is one prompt turn closed by an explicit stop reason, and the capability the core imports exposes exactly that - begin a turn, stream updates as message chunks, tool-call status and plan changes, answer a permission request, cancel, and optionally restore a prior session - expressed in the protocol's vocabulary so any conformant agent can serve without the build writing a client library for it. Cancellation is a first-class contract, not a best-effort kill: a cancelled turn returns the cancelled stop reason and every outstanding permission request resolves as cancelled, and this is proven on every adapter rather than on the one that happens to be interactive. A second adapter has no interactive client at all - a headless or batch runner reached over a remote transport - which is what proves the interface never assumed a live editor, a human at a prompt, or a callback the batch runner cannot provide. Budget, identity and delegation, deterministic pre-turn policy, telemetry and provenance attach to the turn itself, so a turn started from a schedule carries the same guarantees as one a person typed, and permission decisions that a human would have clicked resolve from policy instead of blocking forever.

direction.text: Inside the window the editor-to-agent protocol reached stable version 1 with SDKs in five languages and implementations across dozens of agents and a growing list of editors, and its registry lowered the cost of wiring a new agent in. At the same time a second, host-side open protocol appeared for the host-to-client layer, and the protocol families consolidated under one foundation: 'the industry is signaling a future where these protocols are formally layered and complementary rather than independently competing'. What is settling is the turn as the unit - session setup, prompt turns, streamed messages and tool status, permission requests, file access, terminal execution, cancellation and optional session restoration - and the discipline that a cancelled turn must still return the cancelled stop reason. What is being abandoned is the assumption that agent execution is only ever a local subprocess of an editor: the protocol covers remote agents over HTTP or WebSocket as well as stdio. The sharp edge is that non-interactive sessions cannot answer native permission prompts and need a profile that proceeds headlessly. It would be an error now to define the execution seam so that it requires a live interactive session, a human-answerable permission prompt, or a streaming callback, because that forecloses the headless, scheduled and batch runners the platform must also drive; and equally an error to invent a bespoke per-agent process contract when a stable protocol for the turn exists.
direction.quote: the industry is signaling a future where these protocols are formally layered and complementary rather than independently competing

questions.question: Proposed question: Is agent execution reached through one named capability that cites the protocol and a protocol version, and does every path that runs an agent go through it?
questions.evidence_expected: The interface definition with the protocol version it claims, plus an inventory of every code path that starts agent work showing each resolves through that interface.
questions.aligned_looks_like: One capability, one declared protocol version, and no execution path that spawns an agent by its own means.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Several execution paths with no contract between them; or a contract that names no protocol and no version.

questions.question: Proposed question: Which of the protocol's distinguishing mechanisms are actually used - session setup, a prompt turn closed by a typed stop reason, streamed session updates carrying message chunks and tool-call status, permission requests, and session restoration - and which are stubbed?
questions.evidence_expected: A captured transcript of one real turn showing the update stream and the terminating stop reason, plus the list of protocol methods implemented, stubbed or refused with the reason for each.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The turn ends with a typed stop reason that the caller branches on; updates stream as the turn runs rather than arriving as one final blob; permission requests are real and answered; anything unimplemented is refused explicitly rather than silently ignored.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: The protocol is used as a transport for a single request and reply, stop reasons are collapsed to success or failure, updates are synthesised after the fact, or unimplemented methods fail in undefined ways.

questions.question: Proposed question: How is one turn started, observed, permitted and cancelled from each of the four entries, and what answers a permission request when no human is present?
questions.evidence_expected: The same task run from a human entry, an event, a schedule and an external caller, with the permission exchanges shown for each, and the recorded outcome when a permission request arrived in a non-interactive run.
questions.aligned_looks_like: All four use one path; permission requests in non-interactive runs are resolved deterministically from policy before the turn or answered by a defined non-interactive profile; nothing hangs waiting for a click.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Scheduled or event-driven runs block on a prompt no one can answer, or silently auto-approve everything; or interactive runs use a different code path from the others.

questions.question: Proposed question: Does a second adapter serve the same turn interface without an interactive session - a headless, remote or batch runner - and does one conformance suite pass against both, including cancellation?
questions.evidence_expected: The conformance suite, results against both adapters, and specifically a cancellation case showing the cancelled stop reason returned and outstanding permission requests resolved as cancelled on each.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The second adapter breaks the interactivity assumption rather than being another interactive agent, and cancellation mid-tool-call terminates promptly with the defined result on both.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: One adapter; or a second that is another interactive agent of the same shape; or cancellation that passes on one adapter and hangs or times out on the other.

questions.question: Proposed question: Do the ceiling, the actor with its delegation chain, the deterministic pre-turn policy decision, the telemetry attributes and the provenance record attach to the turn itself without the caller requesting them, and is the criterion a turn is judged against kept out of the turn?
questions.evidence_expected: A telemetry record for one turn showing actor, delegation chain, correlation and budget; a refusal recorded before the turn began; the provenance record for an artifact the turn produced; and the prompt or context actually sent, shown not to contain the grading criterion.
questions.aligned_looks_like: All are applied by the platform, a turn exceeding its ceiling is terminated while the platform continues, refusal precedes spend, and the agent sees its outcome but never the criterion it is judged against.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Budget or identity are optional arguments; refusal happens after the turn has spent tokens; the grading criterion is visible to the agent being graded; or a turn can run with no named actor.

questions.question: Proposed question: Is the seam positioned to survive the layering that is consolidating - a turn interface that neither depends on one agent product nor forecloses a host-side or remote protocol - and is there a written exit if the protocol changes?
questions.evidence_expected: The interface's own types set beside the protocol's message types, an account of which concepts are the build's own and which are borrowed, and the written exit describing what changes if the protocol version moves or a different protocol serves at this layer.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The build owns the turn, the stop reason set and the failure shape; the protocol is a transport an adapter speaks; a version change or a second protocol is confined to adapters.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: The core's types are the protocol's wire messages; or the seam is defined per agent product; or the interface requires a live session, a stream or a human callback that a headless runner could never provide.

gaps.claim: Whether the protocol itself defines a non-interactive or policy-answered permission mode, as opposed to implementations adding one.
gaps.research_query: Agent Client Protocol specification non-interactive permission mode automatic approval headless clients

gaps.claim: Whether a conformance test suite published by the protocol's stewards exists that an adapter can be run against.

standard.name: Model Context Protocol
standard.why: No competing specification for how an agent reaches an external tool surfaced in the window, and the protocol kept shipping: the 2026-07-28 revision made the protocol core stateless, replaced server-initiated requests with a multi-round-trip pattern, added header-based routing, cacheable list results, authorization hardening and a formal extensions framework, and it now sits under Linux Foundation stewardship alongside the other agent protocols, which are being layered rather than set against each other. The remaining question is therefore depth: whether the authorization, transport and discovery mechanisms the revision mandates are actually used.

future_state.text: The proposed future state: every external tool an agent can reach is reached through the protocol and nothing else, with remote servers on the single streamable HTTP transport, authorization by OAuth 2.1 with PKCE, discovery through protected-resource and authorization-server metadata, and resource indicators binding every token - on refresh as well as on issue - to the one server it is for, so a token stolen from one tool surface is useless against another. Interactions that need something back from the client use the multi-round-trip pattern rather than server-initiated requests, so a server can be an ordinary stateless HTTP workload and can be scaled, replaced or hosted anywhere without the core noticing. Tool results are structured against declared output schemas rather than parsed from prose, and tool exposure is progressive: what enters a turn's context is selected by search or by declared toolset rather than by loading every definition, so context cost stays roughly flat as the number of reachable tools grows by an order of magnitude. Every tool call carries a named actor and delegation chain, a deterministic policy decision taken per tool and per actor before the call, a ceiling, correlation attributes and a provenance record, and any tool call with an outward effect carries an idempotency key so a replayed trigger cannot double-act.

direction.text: Inside the window the protocol's centre of gravity moved to stateless remote servers: the 2026-07-28 revision brought a stateless protocol core, header-based routing, cacheable list results and a formal extensions framework, and 'a remote MCP server is now no different from any other HTTP workload'. Two things are being abandoned outright. The older event-stream transport was deprecated in favour of a single streamable HTTP transport, and the server-initiated request pattern was replaced: the multi-round-trip pattern 'replaced server-initiated requests so that elicitation and similar flows work on stateless servers'. Authorization has hardened from optional to mandatory - OAuth 2.1 with PKCE for all remote clients, protected-resource and authorization-server metadata for discovery, and resource indicators so tokens are bound to a specific server, with omission of the resource indicator on refresh identified as a common path to unbound tokens in production. The third thing settling is discovery at scale: a server exposing 400 tools costs over 400,000 tokens before a query is processed, while progressive or semantic discovery holds initial usage roughly flat from 40 tools to 400. It would be an error now to build on the deprecated event-stream transport, to design flows that require a sticky session on the server, to treat authorization as optional or to skip resource indicators on refresh, or to load every tool definition into every turn.
direction.quote: replaced server-initiated requests so that elicitation and similar flows work on stateless servers

questions.question: Proposed question: Is every external tool an agent can reach exposed through the protocol, with a declared protocol revision, and is there any other way for an agent to call out?
questions.evidence_expected: The declared protocol revision, the list of tool surfaces reachable by an agent, and evidence that no direct outward call path exists beside them.
questions.aligned_looks_like: One protocol, one declared revision, and every outward tool call goes through it - including internal ones, which are servers like any other.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Some tools are reached through the protocol and others through bespoke calls; or no revision is declared so it cannot be judged which mechanisms apply.

questions.question: Proposed question: For remote tool surfaces, which authorization and transport mechanisms are actually in force - the streamable transport rather than the deprecated event stream, OAuth 2.1 with PKCE, protected-resource and authorization-server metadata discovery, and resource indicators binding the token to one server on issue and on refresh?
questions.evidence_expected: A captured authorization exchange for one remote surface including the refresh, showing the resource indicator present in both; and the transport actually negotiated.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Every mechanism is present and verified from the exchange itself, including the resource indicator on refresh, and tool results are validated against declared output schemas rather than read as prose.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: The deprecated event-stream transport is in use; authorization is a shared secret or a bearer token with no audience binding; the resource indicator is present on issue but dropped on refresh; results are parsed out of free text.

questions.question: Proposed question: How does a caller cause a tool to be used from each of the four entries, and how is tool exposure decided for a given turn as the number of reachable tools grows?
questions.evidence_expected: The same tool-using task driven from a human entry, an event, a schedule and an external caller; plus a measurement of context tokens consumed by tool definitions at two very different toolset sizes.
questions.aligned_looks_like: One path serves all four; the set of tools entering a turn is selected by declared toolset or by search, and measured context cost is roughly flat as the catalogue grows by an order of magnitude.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Every reachable tool definition is loaded into every turn, so context cost grows with the catalogue and selection accuracy falls; or each entry wires tools differently.

questions.question: Proposed question: Are policy, identity and delegation, budget, correlation, provenance and replay-safety applied to every tool call by the platform, with the decision taken per tool and per actor before the call rather than after?
questions.evidence_expected: A refusal record showing a tool call denied before execution with the actor, tool and rule identified; a telemetry record for an allowed call carrying actor, delegation chain, correlation and cost; and a replayed externally triggered call shown to have had no second effect.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Refusal is deterministic and precedes any outward effect; the delegated agent actor is named distinctly from the human who authorised it; outward-effecting calls carry idempotency keys.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Policy is enforced inside individual tool servers or after the effect; the agent's calls are attributed to a human with no delegation chain; a replayed trigger causes the tool to act twice.

questions.question: Proposed question: Does the tool-access capability sit behind an interface with a proven second implementation, so that swapping a tool surface - or the client that speaks the protocol - is not a core change?
questions.evidence_expected: The conformance suite for the capability, results against two implementations that differ in more than their catalogue, and evidence the core references no implementation directly.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The second implementation differs in execution model - for example a locally hosted surface against a remote one behind full authorization - and the same suite passes against both unmodified.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: There is one client or one server treated as the tool layer; or the core imports a specific server's client code; or the second implementation is the same server run twice.

questions.question: Proposed question: Is the build free of the patterns the window has ruled out - the deprecated transport, flows that need a sticky server session, optional authorization, unbounded tool exposure - and is it positioned for the stateless, extension-framed direction the revision set?
questions.evidence_expected: A statement per pattern of whether it is present, with the configuration or transcript that proves it; plus a demonstration that a tool server can be restarted or replaced mid-conversation without breaking a turn.
questions.aligned_looks_like: None of the ruled-out patterns is present; a server can be scaled or replaced between round trips because nothing depends on server-side session affinity; extensions are declared through the framework rather than as private fields.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Anything that requires a server to hold conversational state; the deprecated transport; authorization treated as optional for internal surfaces; or private protocol extensions invented instead of declared.

gaps.claim: Whether the 2026-07-28 revision mandates or merely enables a declared toolset or search-based discovery mechanism, as opposed to that being a client-side practice.
gaps.research_query: Model Context Protocol 2026-07-28 specification tool discovery toolsets pagination cacheable list results normative requirements

gaps.claim: What proportion of production remote tool surfaces actually enforce audience-bound tokens on refresh.
gaps.research_query: measured survey remote MCP servers resource indicator enforcement refresh tokens 2026

standard.name: Agent Skills spec
standard.why: The packaging specification was published as an open standard in December 2025, is stewarded through the Agentic AI Foundation, and inside the window was implemented across the ecosystem - roughly 40 products on its showcase by June 2026, including OpenAI, Microsoft, JetBrains, Cursor, Google's Gemini CLI, Block's Goose and data platforms - with no competing packaging specification appearing. Its claimed property is that a package written to the spec runs across compatible platforms without modification, so the open question is not which spec but whether the three-tier load and the integrity story are actually used.

future_state.text: The proposed future state: a reusable capability is a portable directory - a manifest carrying at minimum a name and a description, instructions in the body, and optional subdirectories for executable code, reference material and assets - that any conformant runtime can discover and load without the build writing a loader for it. Loading is tiered and the tiers are measured, not asserted: only name and description are resident, the body loads when the capability is triggered, and reference material loads only when the work reaches it, with the resident cost per package counted so a large catalogue has a known context price. Packages are addressed by name and a version constraint through a resolver rather than by a filesystem path joined in code, are versioned semantically so a breaking change is visible before it is loaded, and are resolved only after an integrity digest matches and a publisher signature verifies, because open registries at six-figure scale carry unvetted and sometimes malicious entries. The same resolver serves a local directory and a remote registry behind one interface, and a resolution and a load are where policy, provenance and telemetry attach, so what an agent loaded is as attributable as what it produced.

direction.text: Inside the window packaging went from one vendor's convention to a foundation-stewarded open standard with roughly 40 conformant products, and the claimed property became portability: a package written to the spec runs across compatible platforms without modification. Distribution followed at a scale nobody governs - four registries offering 64K, 91K, 36K and 288K packages respectively as of May 2026, with a scan of 42,447 finding 26.1% carrying at least one security vulnerability. That is the gap the window is closing: registries 'operate like early-era package managers: open submission, minimal vetting, no code signing, no provenance tracking', and the stated remedy is that 'Skill integrity should be treated the same way the software industry treats package integrity through cryptographic signing and verified provenance, with agent runtimes requiring that skills are signed by a known and trusted publisher'. The trajectory named is toward curated, audited registries, semantic versioning of packages, and broader cross-platform portability. It would be an error now to build a loader that joins filesystem paths to find a capability, to copy packages between repositories instead of resolving them by name and version, to invent a private package format when a portable one exists, or to load third-party packages into a privileged agent without a digest and a signature check.
direction.quote: Skill integrity should be treated the same way the software industry treats package integrity through cryptographic signing and verified provenance

questions.question: Proposed question: Are reusable capabilities packaged in the portable directory shape the specification defines - a manifest with the required frontmatter fields, a body, and optional executable, reference and asset subdirectories - such that a runtime the build does not control could load one unchanged?
questions.evidence_expected: One package's directory listing and manifest, plus the specification version it claims, and a statement of any field or layout the build added beyond the spec.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The shape is the spec's, the required fields are present and meaningful, and any addition is an optional extra that a conformant runtime can ignore without the package breaking.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Packages carry a private format, or depend on fields or a directory layout no other runtime would understand, so portability is claimed but untestable.

questions.question: Proposed question: Is loading actually tiered - metadata resident, body on trigger, references on demand - and what is the measured resident cost per package and the cost of a full load?
questions.evidence_expected: A measurement of tokens or bytes resident per package across the whole catalogue, plus a trace of one task showing when the body and then a reference file were loaded.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The three tiers are observable in a real run, the resident cost per package is a measured number rather than an estimate, and reference material demonstrably does not enter context until it is needed.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Everything in the package is loaded whenever the package is available; or the tiers exist in the file layout but the runtime concatenates them anyway; or nobody has measured the resident cost.

questions.question: Proposed question: Before a package is loaded, is its integrity digest matched and its publisher signature verified, is the load decision a policy decision, and is what was loaded recorded in the provenance of whatever the run produced?
questions.evidence_expected: The resolution record for one load showing the name, the version constraint, the resolved version, the digest and the signature verification result; a refusal for an unsigned or digest-mismatched package; and an artifact's provenance record naming the packages in force when it was produced.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Verification is mandatory and precedes load, a failure is a deterministic refusal rather than a warning, and the set of packages in force is part of what an artifact is attributable to.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Packages are loaded from wherever they were found with no digest or signature check; verification is advisory; or an artifact cannot be traced back to the package versions that shaped it.

questions.question: Proposed question: Is a package resolved by name and a version constraint through one resolver that can serve both a local directory and a remote registry, and is the second source proven rather than planned?
questions.evidence_expected: The resolver interface, a conformance run against both a directory source and a registry source, and a search of the executing code for path joins used to locate a package.
questions.aligned_looks_like: One resolution point, two sources differing in where the bytes come from and what identity means, both passing the same suite, and no component constructing a path to find a package.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Loading is a filesystem walk in several components; or a registry source is described as future work; or the second source is the same directory mounted elsewhere.

questions.question: Proposed question: How does a capability get selected and loaded for work arriving from each of the four entries, and how do two packages compose when a task needs both?
questions.evidence_expected: The same task driven from a human entry, an event, a schedule and an external caller with the packages loaded in each recorded; plus one task requiring two packages, showing the order, the combined resident cost and how a conflict between them was resolved.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Selection is the same mechanism at every entry and does not depend on a human describing which package to use; composition is defined, and a conflict has a stated resolution rather than last-writer-wins.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Packages load only for interactive work, or a scheduled run must name files explicitly while a human's run does not; composition is undefined and two packages silently contradict each other.

questions.question: Proposed question: Are packages versioned so a breaking change is visible before load, and is there a way to withdraw or roll back a bad version - the governance the open registries lack?
questions.evidence_expected: The version scheme in use with an example of a breaking change and how it was signalled, the record of a rollback or withdrawal, and the resolution behaviour for a consumer pinned to a withdrawn version.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Versions separate breaking changes from compatible additions and safe fixes, consumers resolve by constraint, and a withdrawn version stops resolving while existing pins get a deterministic refusal rather than silence.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Packages are unversioned or versioned only by edit date; a change is shipped by editing a package in place; there is no way to take a bad version back, and consumers cannot tell what they got.

gaps.claim: Whether the packaging specification itself defines a version field, a digest or a signature mechanism, as opposed to registries and runtimes adding these around it.
gaps.research_query: Agent Skills specification manifest fields version integrity digest signature normative requirements 2026

gaps.claim: Whether any registry inside the window actually enforces publisher signing and transparency-log provenance in production.
gaps.research_query: agent skill registry enforcing publisher signing transparency log provenance production 2026

standard.name: A2A messaging · CloudEvents
standard.why: Two published standards are live for the same job of getting a unit of work in, and neither has displaced the other. CloudEvents is a CNCF graduated project (graduated 25 January 2024) whose current revision v1.0.2 is backward compatible and unchanged inside the window, which makes it the settled envelope for the event and schedule doors. A2A reached v1.0 in April 2026 under the Linux Foundation with over 150 organisations, and v1.0.1 in May 2026 added an extension mechanism, which makes it the leading but recently-versioned choice for the external-agent door. The ecosystem map for 2026 still lists MCP, A2A, ACP and UCP as separate live protocols under institutional rather than technical convergence, both MCP and A2A having moved under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation. So the future state names the property to hold, one normalised envelope behind every door, rather than a winner.

future_state.text: Proposed: inside this window a build normalises all four arrivals — a person, a system event, a timer, an outside system or agent — into one internal work envelope at the intake boundary, so the core sees one shape and cannot tell which door was used. The envelope's identity, source, type, subject, time and payload fields are those of a published event envelope standard rather than invented, and the external-agent door speaks a published agent messaging standard whole: a fetchable capability description an outside caller can read without shared code, an explicit task lifecycle with named terminal states, a subscription or streaming path for work that outlives one request, and a cancellation operation. Correlation and idempotency keys are carried as declared extension attributes on the envelope, set by the boundary and not by the caller, so every downstream guarantee has something stable to hang on. Adding a producer is adding a producer, never a new door.

direction.text: Inside the window the external door consolidated onto foundation-governed protocols rather than converging into one: A2A reached v1.0 in April 2026 under the Linux Foundation with over 150 organisations and added an extension mechanism in v1.0.1, and both MCP and A2A now sit under the Agentic AI Foundation launched in December 2025, described as institutional rather than true protocol convergence. The event side did not move: CloudEvents stayed at a backward-compatible v1.0.2 with graduated status, and its distributed-tracing extension is the sanctioned way to carry context across the event door. What is being abandoned is explicit: Custom HTTP endpoints for agent communication in 2026 are creating technical debt. It would be an error now to define a bespoke intake payload per door, to let one door's wire format become the internal shape, or to treat the external-agent door as a private webhook contract that requires the caller to adopt code from this side.
direction.quote: Custom HTTP endpoints for agent communication in 2026 are creating technical debt.

questions.question: Proposed: Is every arrival represented by an envelope whose attributes come from a published event envelope or agent messaging standard, and is there a machine-readable description of the work this system accepts that an outside caller can fetch?
questions.evidence_expected: One captured envelope per entry (human, event, schedule, external), plus the fetched capability description document and the schema or specification section each envelope claims to conform to.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Each captured envelope validates against the published standard's own schema, and the capability description is retrieved over the wire by a caller holding nothing from this side.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Envelopes are a local structure that borrows a few attribute names from the standard, or the only description of what is accepted is prose written for people.

questions.question: Proposed: Are the mechanisms that separate deep use from a label in use: an explicit task lifecycle that reaches named terminal states including cancelled and rejected, a subscription or streaming path for work that outlives a request, declared extension attributes for correlation and idempotency, and deliberate handling of the envelope's content modes?
questions.evidence_expected: A transcript of one long-running submission showing every state transition to a terminal state; the cancellation of a second submission mid-flight; one envelope shown in both content modes with its extension attributes named.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Terminal states are distinguished from each other and acted on differently, cancellation actually stops work rather than being recorded, and correlation and idempotency ride in named extension attributes rather than in the payload.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Every submission ends in a single generic completed or failed state, long work is polled by the caller because no subscription exists, or correlation is buried inside the free-form payload where no intermediary can read it.

questions.question: Proposed: Does the core import an intake interface rather than any producer, and is there a second conformant producer proving the first is not load-bearing?
questions.evidence_expected: The interface definition, the list of producers behind it, and the diff of the change that added the second producer.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The second producer differs in kind from the first, not merely in vendor, and adding it changed no file the core owns.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Only one producer exists, or the second is the same transport with different configuration, or core code branches on which producer supplied the work.

questions.question: Proposed: Submitted through each of the four entries, does one and the same declared unit of work yield the same normalised envelope apart from the fields that name the door, and the same result?
questions.evidence_expected: Four envelopes and four results from one document driven through the human, event, schedule and external entries, diffed field by field.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The diff is confined to source, entry and time fields; the identity of the work, the payload and the result are identical, and the core path taken is the same.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: A door adds or omits fields the others do not, or one door reaches a different code path, or the same work has to be expressed differently to enter by a different door.

questions.question: Proposed: Do identity, correlation, idempotency and budget attach to the envelope at the intake boundary without the caller supplying or requesting them, and are they attached identically at every door?
questions.evidence_expected: For each door, the envelope as the producer sent it and the envelope as the core received it, showing which fields the boundary added.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The boundary adds the actor, the correlation key, the idempotency key and the ceiling at every door; a caller that omits all of them still gets them, and a caller that supplies a hostile value cannot override the boundary's.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: A guarantee is present at one door and absent at another, or an envelope reaches the core with no actor or no ceiling because the producer did not set one.

questions.question: Proposed: Is the external-agent door a versioned, publicly specified protocol whose revision is negotiated per exchange, or an endpoint shaped for the callers currently known?
questions.evidence_expected: The protocol name and revision served, the refusal returned for an unsupported revision, and the record of an integration completed by a caller who wrote no code from this side.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The served revision is stated on the wire and an unsupported one is refused explicitly; a caller integrates from the published specification alone.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: The door is a hand-rolled HTTP endpoint with per-caller payloads, or the protocol revision is assumed rather than declared, so a caller on a different revision fails in an unspecified way.

gaps.claim: What operators running hundreds of concurrent agents actually use for work intake at scale, and whether they normalise the four doors into one envelope or keep them separate.
gaps.research_query: production multi-agent platform 2026 architecture hundreds of agents work intake normalisation CloudEvents A2A case study

gaps.claim: Whether the agent messaging standard's extension mechanism is in practice used to carry idempotency keys and budget ceilings, or whether implementers put them in the payload.
gaps.research_query: A2A extension mechanism 1.0.1 examples idempotency key budget metadata extension registry usage 2026

standard.name: JSON Schema 2020-12
standard.why: 2020-12 is still the latest published release inside the window, and the standardisation work in flight is a re-consolidation of it rather than a successor: the IETF working-group draft is described as little more than an edit of 2020-12, recombining Core, Validation and Hyper-Schema into one document, and it expires 27 February 2027. There is no competing cross-language declared-shape standard; the live alternatives are code-first validators bound to one language, and even those converge on the dialect as the interchange form, with Zod 4.3 adding fromJSONSchema() and the standing advice being that a single source of truth shared with backends, third-party clients or OpenAPI generators stays on a JSON Schema validator such as Ajv. A published, language-agnostic conformance suite exists, so the question is not which standard but how deeply it is used.

future_state.text: Proposed: inside this window every document that crosses a boundary — each door's envelope, the declared unit of work, the plan, the result, the verdict — declares its shape in the published dialect and is checked at that boundary by an interchangeable validator the core reaches only through an interface. The schemas use the dialect's own machinery rather than a keyword subset: a declared identifier and dialect on every schema, references and dynamic references for reuse and recursion instead of copied fragments, unevaluated-property closure so composition cannot silently admit unknown fields, explicitly declared vocabularies, and the assertion form of format wherever a format must reject rather than annotate. Validation returns a structured output unit naming the instance location and the schema location that failed, which is rendered into the platform's typed failure object rather than a string; it is applied by the platform and cannot be declined, no component hand-rolls field checks behind it, and whether a candidate validator may serve is decided by running the published language-agnostic conformance suite and recording the result.

direction.text: The dialect is stable and the movement inside the window is procedural, not technical: The current version is 2020-12, which was the latest published release, and the IETF draft carrying it forward is little more than an edit of 2020-12 that re-combines Core, Validation and Hyper-Schema into one document, expiring 27 February 2027. So targeting 2020-12 now, and treating the meta-schema identifier as the version handle so a later dialect is a declaration change, is the aligned bet. The pressure comes from code-first validators — Zod, Valibot, Joi, CUE — which are faster to write in one language but do not produce a shared artefact; the reported convergence runs the other way, with Zod 4.3 adding fromJSONSchema() to consume schemas and the advice for one source of truth shared with backends and third-party clients remaining a standards-compliant validator such as Ajv. It would be an error now to pin to a pre-2020-12 draft, to define shapes only in one language's type system, to hand-roll keyword checks inside components, or to treat format as a rejection when the default vocabulary makes it an annotation.
direction.quote: The current version is 2020-12, which was the latest published release.

questions.question: Proposed: Does every document that crosses a boundary have a schema in the published dialect, and does each schema declare the dialect it is written in?
questions.evidence_expected: The set of boundary document types, the schema for each, and the declared dialect identifier at the head of each schema.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Every boundary document type has a schema, each names 2020-12 explicitly, and there is no document type entering the system without one.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Schemas exist for some document types only, or the dialect is left implicit and inferred by whichever validator happens to load it.

questions.question: Proposed: Are the dialect's distinguishing mechanisms in use — identifiers and references for reuse, dynamic references for recursive or extensible shapes, unevaluated-property closure under composition, declared vocabularies, and the assertion form of format where a format must reject — or is the schema a flat list of types and required fields?
questions.evidence_expected: The schemas themselves, plus one instance that a naive keyword-subset check would accept and the declared schema rejects, with the validator output for it.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Composition keywords are closed with unevaluated-property handling, shared fragments are referenced rather than copied, and a format that must reject is under the assertion vocabulary and demonstrably rejects.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Schemas use only type, properties and required, composition leaves unknown fields admitted, formats are relied on to reject while the default annotation vocabulary is in force, or fragments are duplicated across schemas and have drifted.

questions.question: Proposed: Does the core import a validation interface rather than a validator, and has a second validator with a different execution model been run against the same schemas and instances?
questions.evidence_expected: The interface definition, the two adapters, and the recorded output of the published language-agnostic conformance suite for each.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Both validators pass the same conformance run and agree on the same corpus of instances; swapping which one serves is a configuration change with no core diff.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: One validator only, or the second is the same engine wrapped differently, or core code calls validator-specific APIs or reads validator-specific error text.

questions.question: Proposed: Does a caller at every entry get the same validation outcome for the same malformed document, and does the failure name the exact location in the instance and in the schema?
questions.evidence_expected: One deliberately malformed document submitted through the human, event, schedule and external entries, and the four failure objects returned.
questions.aligned_looks_like: All four failures carry the same type, the same instance location and the same schema location, and a machine can act on them without reading prose.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: One entry returns a validation failure and another accepts the document or fails later during execution; or the failure is a message a caller must parse to learn which field was wrong.

questions.question: Proposed: Is validation applied by the platform at the boundary so no caller and no component can decline it, and is the refusal it produces recorded and attributable like any other refusal?
questions.evidence_expected: The wiring that shows where validation is invoked, an attempt to submit work bypassing it, and the record left behind by a rejected document.
questions.aligned_looks_like: There is exactly one place a document can enter, validation there is unconditional, and a rejection is recorded with the actor and the correlation key before any spend.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: A path exists that skips validation, or a component re-checks fields itself because it does not trust the boundary, or a rejection leaves no record.

questions.question: Proposed: Is the dialect version a declaration that can be changed, and is the shape of a document defined once in the published dialect rather than in one language's type system with the schema derived as an afterthought?
questions.evidence_expected: The single place the dialect identifier is stated, and the generation direction between the schemas and any language-level types.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Schemas are the source of truth and language types are generated from them; the dialect identifier appears in one place and a change to it is a declaration change.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Types in one language are the source and schemas are exported for documentation only, or the dialect identifier is hard-coded across many files, or a pre-2020-12 draft is still targeted.

gaps.claim: Whether the standardised output formats of the dialect are implemented consistently enough across validators that a failure object can be built from them without validator-specific handling.
gaps.research_query: JSON Schema 2020-12 output format basic detailed verbose validator support comparison 2026 interoperability

gaps.claim: How large agent platforms validate documents whose shape is only known at run time, where a schema must be resolved per unit of work rather than compiled once.
