standard.name: OTLP · GenAI semantic conventions
standard.why: The wire protocol has no credible competitor: OTLP is the vendor-neutral wire protocol behind a CNCF graduated project described as the default instrumentation standard for cloud-native systems in 2026, with the CNCF 2025 survey published January 2026 reporting 49% running OpenTelemetry in production and 26% evaluating, and the payoff that switching backends is a configuration change, not a code change. The layer above it is not equally settled and this matters for how the questions are asked: on 12 June 2026 the GenAI conventions were moved out of the main semantic-conventions repository into a dedicated one with its own cadence, and as of 17 July 2026 no GenAI span, event, metric or attribute is marked Stable. So the transport is baseline and the attribute vocabulary is pre-stable, and the future state asks for depth against the transport and version-pinned tolerance against the vocabulary.

future_state.text: Proposed: inside this window all three signals leave the platform over the standard telemetry protocol to a collector the platform owns, so which backend receives them is a configuration change and never a code change, and no caller chooses or declines it. Agent work is emitted as the span tree the conventions prescribe — a run span parenting each model call and each tool call, with the operation name, model, token counts and cost as attributes on the spans that own them — so the shape of one exported trace is enough to tell real instrumentation from a library that was merely installed. Because the generative-AI attribute vocabulary is still pre-stable, the emitted convention version is pinned and declared in one place with the opt-in switch the specification provides, so a rename absorbed upstream is a configuration change. Correlation across asynchronous, resumed and scheduled work rides on explicit correlation attributes carried in the work envelope rather than on trace parentage, so a unit resumed hours later still joins its predecessors, and refusals, budget terminations and verdicts are spans and events too, not only log lines.

direction.text: The transport is settled and the vocabulary is moving. Inside the window the generative-AI conventions were separated from the main semantic-conventions release on 12 June 2026 at v1.42.0 into a dedicated repository with no tagged release, and as of 17 July 2026 the GenAI conventions remain Development, with no timeline to stable and OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN as the sanctioned way to absorb transitions. Meanwhile the shape settled even where the names did not: the conventions model the whole agent execution as a span tree, with invoke_agent as the parent span containing chat spans for each model call and execute_tool spans for each tool invocation, and named operations covering create_agent, invoke_workflow, retrieval, plan and memory. What is being abandoned is proprietary instrumentation and vendor SDK lock-in, since OTel has largely solved that problem in 2026. It would be an error now to instrument through a vendor's own SDK, to treat the pre-stable attribute names as frozen, or to rely on trace parentage across asynchronous agent hops, where trace context often doesn't automatically transfer and the result is two disconnected traces instead of one continuous workflow.
direction.quote: the GenAI conventions remain Development

questions.question: Proposed: Do traces, metrics and logs all leave the platform over the standard telemetry protocol, or only some of them, and is the receiving backend named anywhere the core can see?
questions.evidence_expected: The exporter configuration, one exported payload per signal captured at the wire, and a search of core code for the backend's name.
questions.aligned_looks_like: All three signals are exported over the standard protocol to a collector, and the backend appears only in configuration.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Only traces are exported while cost and refusal data live in ad hoc logs, or a backend's client library is imported by code that does the work.

questions.question: Proposed: Does one exported trace of one unit of agent work show the span tree the conventions prescribe — a run span parenting model-call spans and tool-call spans, each with its operation name — with token counts and cost attributes on the spans that own them?
questions.evidence_expected: One exported trace for a unit of work that made at least two model calls and one tool call, with all spans and attributes.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The tree matches the prescribed parent-child shape, operation names come from the published set, and token and cost attributes sit on the model spans rather than being summed at the top.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: The whole unit is one flat span, or spans are named locally rather than by the convention's operation names, or cost is a single number attached at the end with no per-call attribution.

questions.question: Proposed: Is the telemetry backend replaceable by configuration alone, demonstrated rather than asserted, with the core importing an emission interface and never a backend client?
questions.evidence_expected: The record of one run exported to two different receivers, the diff of the change that switched them, and the emission interface definition.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The switch is a configuration diff with no change to code that does work, and both receivers show the same spans and attributes.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Switching required code changes, or the second receiver is the same product in another deployment, or attributes are shaped to suit one backend's query language.

questions.evidence_expected: Traces for one unit of work that crossed a process boundary and was resumed after a delay, plus an attempt to run a unit with telemetry not requested.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The resumed unit and its predecessor are joinable by an explicit correlation attribute present on every span, and a caller who asks for nothing is still fully instrumented.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Work resumed across an asynchronous boundary appears as a disconnected second trace, or instrumentation depends on the caller passing a context, or a caller can opt out.

questions.evidence_expected: Four traces, one per entry, and the queries used to answer each of those questions from them.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The same query answers all four, and refusals and budget terminations appear as spans or events with a reason attribute, not only in prose logs.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: The question is answerable for the human entry but not for the scheduled or external one, or answering it requires joining exported telemetry with a private log file.

questions.evidence_expected: The single declaration of the emitted convention version, and the record of one convention change absorbed, or a written statement of how one would be.

standard.name: Rego / OPA
standard.why: Two or more decision languages are live and the thing that settled inside the window is the interface between them, not a winner. OPA is a CNCF graduated project (graduated 29 January 2021) whose engine evaluates structured queries in Rego and returns structured decisions any system can act on, but its commercial sponsor wound down after an August 2025 acqui-hire of its creators, and Cedar is a live, analysable alternative benchmarked 42.8x-80.8x faster than Rego on the same authorization scenarios. In March 2026, inside the window, the AuthZEN Authorization API 1.0 was published as a Standards Track specification standardising the request and response between policy enforcement points and decision points while deliberately avoiding the decision method, so that behind it organizations can continue using RBAC, ABAC, ReBAC, XACML, graph-based approaches, Rego, Cedar, or even fully proprietary engines. The property to hold is therefore a language-neutral decision call, not a language.

future_state.text: Proposed: inside this window policy is a decision service reached through a capability interface whose request and response follow the published, language-neutral authorization decision API, so the language a rule is written in is an adapter choice and a second engine in a different language proves the first is not load-bearing. The input document is assembled by the platform, not by the caller — the actor and its delegation chain, the action, the resource, the tenant, the entry it arrived by, and the budget remaining — so a caller cannot shape the question to get the answer it wants. Every decision is evaluated before any spend or side effect and is deterministic: the same input yields the same decision, and a decision that cannot be reached is a refusal rather than an allow. Every decision emits a structured decision record carrying the input, the result, a decision identifier and the version of the policy bundle that produced it, so a refusal is auditable and replayable months later; policies are distributed as versioned, signed, immutable bundles rather than files edited in place; and a refusal is returned to the caller as the platform's typed failure object naming the rule that refused, never as prose.

direction.text: The direction inside the window is that the decision interface standardised while the decision languages did not. AuthZEN 1.0 was published as a Standards Track specification in March 2026 as the protocol for authorization request and response between policy enforcement points and decision points, and it deliberately avoids the decision method, unlike XACML which standardised both: Behind an AuthZEN interface, organizations can continue using RBAC, ABAC, ReBAC, XACML, graph-based approaches, Rego, Cedar, or even fully proprietary engines. Rego's engine remains CNCF graduated but its commercial sponsor wound down after an August 2025 acqui-hire, while Cedar is reported 42.8x-80.8x faster on equivalent scenarios and is restricted and analysable by design; the pattern most cited for agent runtimes is a decision point fronting the tool gateway, answering in well under a millisecond, which removes performance as an argument for deciding after the fact. It would be an error now to embed policy as conditionals in the code that acts, to bind the core to one engine's query API or one language's syntax, to evaluate after spend, or to let a caller assemble the input document it will be judged on.
direction.quote: this simple JSON-based API is the long-awaited standard protocol for authorization request/response communication between policy enforcement points and decision points

questions.question: Proposed: Are policy rules expressed as data evaluated by a decision engine, separate from the code that acts, and is there a single decision call every enforcement point makes?
questions.evidence_expected: The policy sources, the decision call signature, and a search of acting code for conditionals that grant or deny.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Rules live outside the acting code in a declarative form, and every enforcement point reaches the same decision call.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Permission logic is spread through conditionals in the code that performs the action, or several components each decide for themselves.

questions.question: Proposed: Are the mechanisms that separate deep use from a rules file in use: versioned distributable policy bundles rather than files edited in place, a structured decision record per query carrying the input, result, decision identifier and bundle version, and a decision input document assembled by the platform?
questions.evidence_expected: One decision record for a real refusal, the bundle version it names, the manifest of that bundle, and the code path that builds the input document.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The refusal can be replayed later from its record against the exact bundle version that produced it, and the input document is built from platform-held facts about the actor and the unit of work.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Policies are loose files loaded from disk with no version, decisions leave no record beyond an allow or deny boolean, or the caller passes in the attributes it will be judged on.

questions.question: Proposed: Does the core import a decision interface whose request and response follow the published language-neutral decision API, with a second engine in a different policy language proved against the same decision corpus?
questions.evidence_expected: The interface definition, the two engine adapters, and the recorded run of a shared corpus of decisions against both.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Both engines answer the same corpus identically through the same request shape; the second engine uses a genuinely different language, and swapping is a configuration change.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: The interface mirrors one engine's own query API, the second engine is the same one deployed differently, or no second engine has ever been run.

questions.question: Proposed: Does the decision happen before any spend or side effect, and does its input carry the actor and delegation chain, the tenant and the remaining budget without the caller supplying them?
questions.evidence_expected: A trace of one refused unit of work showing the ordering of the decision relative to the first side effect and the first token spent, plus the input document that was evaluated.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The decision span precedes any model call, tool call or write; the input names the acting agent and the human it acts for, and no cost was incurred before the refusal.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Policy is checked after execution or only at the outer edge, the input identifies a service account rather than the delegating actor, or a refused unit still spent budget.

questions.question: Proposed: Is the same decision reached for the same action regardless of which of the four entries requested it, and does a caller receive the refusal in a form it can branch on without reading prose?
questions.evidence_expected: One action that policy refuses, attempted through the human, event, schedule and external entries, and the four responses.
questions.aligned_looks_like: All four are refused identically, and each response carries a typed failure whose type identifies the refusal and whose members name the rule.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: One entry bypasses the decision point, or the scheduled entry runs under a blanket allow, or the refusal is a message a caller must parse.

questions.question: Proposed: Is the decision call shaped by the published, language-neutral decision API rather than by whichever engine is installed, so a change of decision language is an adapter change?
questions.evidence_expected: The decision request and response schema, mapped field by field against the published API, and the list of engine-specific fields that leak through.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The request and response are the published shape; nothing engine-specific appears in the interface, and policy source syntax is confined to the adapter.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: The interface carries an engine's package paths, query strings or result envelope, so the core would have to change to speak to a different engine.

standard.name: in-toto · SLSA · DSSE
standard.why: The three named specifications are one layered format rather than three competitors: in-toto attestations have two layers, the DSSE envelope and the statement, DSSE signing over the payload type and payload together using PAE to prevent confusion attacks, and SLSA provenance is expressed as an in-toto attestation. SLSA v1.1 is the current version and is a minor, backward-compatible release that also adds verification procedures for VSAs. There is no competing attestation format; instead, verification is commodity, with Rekor v2 GA since October 2025 and Cosign v3 (v3.1.1, June 2026) verifying npm provenance, GitHub Artifact Attestations and Homebrew provenance with one tool, and the transparency log accessible to anyone. The generative-AI work inside the window extends this stack rather than replacing it, with AIBOM and action evidence packages emitting in-toto or SLSA provenance statements.

future_state.text: Proposed: inside this window every artifact the platform produces — a plan, a result, a verdict, a file, a decision — carries an attestation in the published statement format, wrapped in the published signing envelope, whose subject is named by cryptographic digest and whose predicate names the code version that produced it, every input by digest, and the actor including the delegated agent actor and the human it acts for. Attestations are appended to a tamper-evident, append-only store that yields an inclusion proof, so a later edit is detectable rather than merely discouraged, and signing is keyless and short-lived rather than resting on a long-lived key an operator holds. The decisive property is external verifiability: a third party holding only the artifact, the attestation and public key material verifies it with a general-purpose verifier and no code from this platform, and that verification is exercised in the pipeline together with a deliberate mutation that makes it fail, so the check is known to be able to fail. The signed record covers what an agent did, who or what authorised it and what came out, captured at the moment of the action rather than reconstructed afterwards from logs.

direction.text: The format is settled and the movement is outward, from build artifacts to agent actions and model artifacts. SLSA v1.1 is a minor, backward-compatible release whose attestation schemas are now explicitly informative, with the specification texts canonical, and it adds procedures for verifying VSAs. Verification became commodity inside and just before the window: Rekor v2 reached GA in October 2025 on a tile-based backend, Cosign v3.1.1 shipped in June 2026 defaulting to the standardised bundle format, and attestations can be verified by any tool that speaks the in-toto and DSSE formats, with PyPI, npm and Maven Central all publishing in this stack. The extension is toward agent evidence: an action evidence package (AEP) is a signed, append-only record of what an AI agent did, who or what authorized the action, and what the outcome was, and AIBOM work emits in-toto or SLSA provenance statements listing exact inputs and parameters rather than inventing a new format. It would be an error now to design a bespoke provenance record, to sign with a long-lived operator-held key instead of short-lived keyless identity, to rely on an append-only file with no inclusion proof, or to ship provenance that only this platform's own code can verify.
direction.quote: An action evidence package (AEP) is a signed, append-only record of what an AI agent did, who or what authorized the action, and what the outcome was

questions.question: Proposed: Does every artifact the platform produces carry an attestation in the published statement format, wrapped in the published signing envelope, or does provenance exist only for some artifact kinds?
questions.evidence_expected: The list of artifact kinds the platform emits, and one attestation for each, shown with its envelope and statement layers.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Every emitted artifact kind has an attestation whose statement names the subject by digest and whose envelope is the published signing format.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Attestations exist for released build outputs only, while plans, verdicts and agent results are recorded as ordinary log lines with no signed statement.

questions.question: Proposed: Does the predicate actually name what would let someone reproduce or dispute the artifact — the code version, every input by digest, the acting agent and the human it acts for, the policy decision and the model used — or only a timestamp and a label?
questions.evidence_expected: One attestation for a real agent-produced artifact, field by field, alongside the inputs it names.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Every input is identified by digest and resolvable; the actor is the delegated agent with its delegating human named; the code version is exact rather than a branch name.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: The predicate carries a name, a time and a free-text description; inputs are referenced by path or by mutable tag, so the same attestation would describe a different artifact tomorrow.

questions.question: Proposed: Can a third party verify an attestation with a general-purpose verifier and public key material alone, with no code from this platform, and has that been demonstrated?
questions.evidence_expected: The recorded output of a verification run using a tool this platform did not write, on an artifact it produced, and the recorded output of the same run against a deliberately mutated artifact.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The independent verifier accepts the genuine artifact and rejects the mutated one, and the failing run is recorded alongside the passing one.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Verification requires a checker from this platform, or only the passing run was ever recorded so the check is not known to be able to fail.

questions.question: Proposed: Is the attestation produced by the platform for every unit of work without the caller asking, and is the store append-only with an integrity mechanism that makes a later edit detectable rather than merely discouraged?
questions.evidence_expected: The store's integrity mechanism, an attempt to alter a past record, and the detection that results; plus one unit of work run by a caller who requested nothing.
questions.aligned_looks_like: A tampered past record is detected by an inclusion or chain proof rather than by convention, and every unit of work is attested whether or not it asked.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: The store is an append-only file with no proof of inclusion, or attestation is a step a caller or a component can skip.

questions.question: Proposed: Starting from one artifact, can an answerer walk the chain back through every unit of work, decision and input that produced it, regardless of which entry started it?
questions.evidence_expected: One artifact produced by a scheduled run that was itself triggered by an event, and the traversal from the artifact to the originating event, with each attestation in between.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The chain is unbroken and machine-traversable across entries and across process boundaries, linked by digests and correlation identifiers rather than by timestamp proximity.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: The chain stops at the last unit of work, or crossing an entry boundary requires a human to reason about which record probably corresponds to which.

questions.question: Proposed: Is signing keyless and short-lived with the identity of the signer bound at signing time, and is the record of what an agent did signed at the moment of the action rather than assembled afterwards from logs?
questions.evidence_expected: The signing configuration and key lifetime, and the point in the execution path where the record is signed relative to the action it describes.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Signing identity is short-lived and bound to the workload, and the record is produced and signed as the action completes, before anything downstream could edit it.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: A long-lived key is held by an operator or a shared secret store, or provenance is reconstructed from logs after the fact, so what is signed is a report rather than evidence.

standard.name: RFC 9457 problem details
standard.why: RFC 9457 is an IETF Standards Track document published July 2023 that obsoletes RFC 7807 and defines a single machine-readable error body served as application/problem+json with five standard members, type, title, status, detail and instance, plus extension members that clients must ignore when unrecognised so problem types can evolve. There is no competing error-body format; in 2026 it is reported as the most widely adopted error format across major APIs including Stripe, GitHub and Cloudflare, with frameworks emitting it natively. What is left is depth: a registry for common problem-type URIs, guidance on returning multiple problems in one response, and handling for non-dereferenceable type URIs, with a formal registry hosted at IANA. So the question is not whether to adopt it but how much of it is used.

future_state.text: Proposed: inside this window every boundary in the platform — each of the four entries, each capability adapter, each refusal, each budget termination, each validation rejection — returns one problem object with the standard members and a type identifier drawn from a closed registry the platform publishes, where identifiers are never reused and each is documented with the extension members it carries. The type identifier, never the status code and never the prose, is what a caller branches on; the human-readable members carry no information a caller needs. Extension members carry what the caller must act on: the correlation identifier, whether the failure is retryable and when, the budget or quota remaining, the instance and schema location of a validation failure, the rule that refused, and the identity of the capability that failed. Multiple problems arising from one request are returned together rather than only the first, and the same problem shape is produced on transports that are not request-and-response, so an event or scheduled arrival yields the same machine-readable failure to its dead-letter path that a synchronous caller receives inline. Nothing hands a stack trace or a log line back to whoever called.

direction.text: The format is settled and the movement inside the window is registry-shaped rather than format-shaped. RFC 9457 obsoletes RFC 7807 as a backward-compatible update that does not define a new format, and its Appendix D additions are a registry for common problem-type URIs, clearer guidance on returning multiple problems in one response, and handling for non-dereferenceable type URIs, with a formal registry hosted at IANA. Adoption in 2026 is reported as the most widely adopted error format across major APIs including Stripe, GitHub and Cloudflare, with frameworks such as ASP.NET Core in .NET 10 and Quarkus emitting it natively, and the RFC 9457 Problem Details standard is recommended for structuring error payloads as part of a 2026 shift toward shared standards. What is being abandoned is the success-shaped error body and status-only signalling: 200-with-error-body is an anti-pattern, retryability is expected to be stated in the body as a retryAfter extension member and a Retry-After header so automated retry libraries can act, and the type field is a URI that uniquely identifies the error, enabling programmatic error handling. It would be an error now to define a bespoke error envelope, to make a caller parse prose or match on a message string, to signal only through a status code, or to mint type identifiers ad hoc with no registry behind them.
direction.quote: 200-with-error-body is an anti-pattern.

questions.question: Proposed: Does every boundary return the standard problem object with its five standard members and its media type, or do some boundaries still return a bespoke error shape?
questions.evidence_expected: One failure captured from each boundary kind: an entry, a capability adapter, a validation rejection, a policy refusal, a budget termination.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Every captured failure is a problem object with the standard members and the correct media type, and no boundary has its own error shape.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: The outer entries return problem objects while internal adapters raise exceptions or return strings that a wrapper turns into prose at the edge.

questions.question: Proposed: Are the type identifiers drawn from a published closed registry with documented extension members per type, and do the extension members carry what a caller must act on — retryability, correlation, the location that failed, the rule that refused — rather than the human-readable members carrying it?
questions.evidence_expected: The registry of type identifiers, and for three different failure kinds the full problem object including extension members.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Each type is registered, stable and documented with its extensions; a caller can decide retry, escalate or correct from the machine-readable members alone with the prose removed.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Type identifiers are minted per throw site or are all one generic value, or the actionable information exists only inside the human-readable detail member.

questions.question: Proposed: Does a caller branch on the type identifier alone, and can the same failure be handled identically whether it arrived through the human, event, schedule or external entry?
questions.evidence_expected: The caller-side handling code, and the four failure objects produced by driving one failing unit of work through each entry.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The handling code matches on type identifiers only; the four objects carry the same type and the same extension members, differing only in instance and correlation.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Handling code matches on a status code, an error message substring, or the name of the component that failed; or one entry loses the failure into a log and returns nothing actionable.

questions.question: Proposed: Does every failure object carry the correlation identifier and the actor without the caller asking, and does a budget termination or a policy refusal arrive as a typed problem rather than as a silent stop?
questions.evidence_expected: The problem object returned for a unit terminated on its ceiling and for a unit refused by policy, plus the telemetry span for each.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Both carry a distinct type, the correlation identifier, and the remaining or exceeded amount as extension members, and both are joinable to their telemetry without a text search.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: A budget termination surfaces as a generic internal failure or as no response at all, or a refusal reaches the caller with no correlation identifier so it cannot be tied to its trace.

questions.question: Proposed: Is the production of the failure object owned by one place the core imports, so a new capability adapter cannot invent its own failure shape?
questions.evidence_expected: The single construction point for problem objects, and a search across adapters for locally constructed error responses.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Adapters raise typed conditions that the shared construction point renders; there is no second place a failure body is built.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Each adapter builds its own body, so shapes drift, or an adapter passes an underlying library's error structure straight through to the caller.

questions.question: Proposed: Is retryability stated in the failure rather than inferred by the caller, and is the same problem shape produced on transports that are not request-and-response?
questions.evidence_expected: A transient failure's problem object with its retry members, and the failure record left for an event-driven or scheduled arrival that had no synchronous caller.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Retryability and the wait are stated explicitly in the body; the asynchronous path records the identical problem object for its dead-letter or failure channel.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Callers infer retryability from a status code or from message text, or asynchronous arrivals fail with only a log line while synchronous ones get a typed body.

standard.name: OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange · workload identity
standard.why: Token exchange itself is a published RFC (RFC 8693) and is described in the window as the standards-based approach for multi-hop agent delegation, but it is not the only live candidate for how an agent obtains on-behalf-of authority: the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG, Cross App Access) reached IETF draft-04 on 2026-05-21 and is being positioned as the enterprise-managed authorization extension for tool access, while the resource side of the same problem is being fixed by RFC 9728 protected resource metadata and RFC 8707 resource indicators. The workload half is equally plural: attested workload identity (SPIFFE/SPIRE JWT-SVIDs) and cloud OIDC federation (Entra ID WIF, AWS STS, GCP IAM Pools) both mint the short-lived credentials a platform needs. Two or more mechanisms are live, so the future state names the property to hold - a verifiable actor plus an explicit acting party on every call - and not the winner.

future_state.text: Every principal - human, workload and agent - is a first-class subject holding a short-lived credential the platform attested rather than a secret an operator configured, and no component mints, parses or validates a credential itself: one identity capability interface offers attest, exchange, attenuate and verify, and the core imports only that. Every outbound call carries a token produced by an exchange step that names both the subject the work is done for and the acting party doing it, because delegation is impossible with only a subject_token and no actor_token; each hop adds one acting-party entry and narrows scope rather than replacing the chain, and each token is bound to the audience of the single resource it is presented to, discovered from that resource rather than configured. Credentials are per-invocation and minutes-long, revocable while work is in flight, and the interface never leaks an issuer's token format upward, so an attestation-based workload identity plane, an OIDC provider, or an assertion-grant issuer can each serve behind it without the core learning which one answered.
future_state.quote: delegation is impossible with only a subject_token and no actor_token

direction.text: Inside the window the resource half settled hard: tool endpoints are now formally OAuth 2.1 resource servers that must publish protected resource metadata (RFC 9728) so a caller discovers the right authorization server, and callers must use resource indicators (RFC 8707) so a token cannot be replayed at a different server - shipped in the 2026-07-28 tool-protocol revision. Cross App Access is the friendly name for an IETF draft called the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG), currently at draft-04 and last updated 2026-05-21, and it is the live alternative for enterprise-mediated on-behalf-of access. Workload identity federation, where an attested JWT-SVID is exchanged at a cloud token service for temporary credentials, is displacing static multi-cloud keys. What is being abandoned: static long-lived API keys per agent, identity agreed once at connect time and never re-checked, and single broad tokens reused across resources. It would be an error now to build a bespoke per-agent key registry, or to mint impersonation-only tokens that erase the acting party, since that forecloses both live delegation mechanisms.

questions.question: Against the proposed future state, is there a single named identity capability interface that every credential passes through, such that no other component obtains, stores or validates a credential of its own?
questions.evidence_expected: The interface definition, plus a search across the rest of the codebase for credential handling and for secrets read from configuration or environment.
questions.aligned_looks_like: One interface with mint/exchange/verify operations; every other component receives an already-scoped credential and holds no secret material.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: No interface at all, or several components each reading their own keys from configuration, so identity is a convention rather than a boundary.

questions.question: The proposed future state turns on deep use, so: in a call made three hops deep, does the presented credential name both the original subject and every acting party in order, or only one identity?
questions.evidence_expected: The decoded claims of a credential captured at the third hop of a real run, alongside the claims at hop one.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Subject preserved from hop one; one acting-party entry added per hop in order; audience and scope strictly narrower at each hop.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: A single subject with no acting party (impersonation), the chain flattened to the most recent actor, or the same broad token forwarded unchanged.

questions.question: The proposed future state turns on deep use, so: are credentials attested at issue time from the running environment and bound to the specific resource they are presented to, or are they long-lived bearer secrets with a broad audience?
questions.evidence_expected: Issue and expiry times from a sample of live credentials, the audience value each carries, and how the resource's authorization server was located.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Minutes-long lifetimes, one audience per resource, the authorization server discovered from the resource rather than hard-coded, and no static secret at rest.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: One token per environment with a wide or absent audience, lifetime measured in days, or endpoints and issuers pinned in configuration.

questions.evidence_expected: The output of one conformance suite run against both issuers, and the change set that performed the swap.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Both pass the same suite; the swap touches only wiring; no issuer-specific claim name or token shape appears above the interface.

questions.question: The guarantee proposed here is applied, not requested, so: which cross-cutting guarantees attach at the moment a credential is issued or exchanged, and can a caller decline any of them?
questions.evidence_expected: The issue path with its policy check, telemetry attributes and recorded evidence, plus an attempt to obtain a credential while bypassing them.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Policy decides before issue, the issue and every exchange are recorded with the actor chain, and the bypass attempt is refused with a typed failure.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Issue is unlogged or unpoliced, or the guarantees are parameters the caller passes and can therefore omit.

questions.evidence_expected: For one unit of work started at each entry: the credential presented at entry, the principal resolved from it, and the credential presented on the first outbound call.

standard.name: RFC 5545 recurrence rules
standard.why: The recurrence grammar has no credible competitor. The same rule parsed by any conforming implementation produces the same result, whereas Vixie cron, systemd timers, AWS EventBridge, Google Cloud Scheduler and GitHub Actions each implement slightly different syntax, so a cron expression is not portable. The nearest alternative, JSCalendar (RFC 8984), positions itself as a successor serialisation for calendar data but its RecurrenceRule object is a JSON mapping of the iCalendar RECUR value type with the same semantics, so it restates the grammar rather than competing with it; conformant libraries continued to appear in the window, including ones extending to RFC 7529 non-Gregorian calendars. The open question is therefore depth of use, not choice of standard.

future_state.text: Every recurring unit of work is declared as a recurrence rule in the standard grammar, stored with an explicit start instant and a named time zone, never as a platform-specific interval string, so that the same rule parsed by any conforming implementation producing the same result is a property the build can rely on when it moves hosts. A schedule is durable, addressable platform state - creatable, inspectable, pausable, editable and backfillable through the same interface at any entry - rather than configuration on a host, and it carries its operational policy with it: what happens when a fire is missed, how far back catch-up may reach, whether overlapping runs are allowed or skipped, and how much jitter spreads a fleet of schedules. Expansion of a rule into concrete fire times sits behind a recurrence capability so the parser can be replaced without touching the core, and each fire produces a unit of work through the same intake path as any other entry, carrying an idempotency key derived from the schedule's identity and the nominal fire time so that a catch-up, an operator backfill and a retry of the same fire converge on one execution.
future_state.quote: the same rule parsed by any conforming implementation producing the same result

direction.text: Inside the window, scheduling moved from host configuration to durable, observable state owned by an execution service: Cadence shipped Schedules in June 2026, where a Schedule lives on the server and can be observed, paused, updated, and backfilled without touching workflow code, with catch-up bounded to a lookback window and dispatch governed by a declared overlap policy; jitter as thundering-herd protection is now discussed as standard practice for scheduled agent workloads. Recurrence-rule services extended the grammar to agent triggers, and conforming RFC 5545 libraries built on modern time-zone-aware date APIs (including RFC 7529 RSCALE support) landed in the window. What is being abandoned: bare per-platform cron strings as the source of truth, and timers with no record of the last fire. It would be an error now to hold schedules only in a host crontab or an in-process timer, to store a rule without its time zone, or to expand recurrence in UTC and treat local wall time as incidental, since the grammar's whole value is portable, zone-correct expansion.
direction.quote: A Schedule lives on the server and can be observed, paused, updated, and backfilled without touching workflow code

questions.question: Against the proposed future state, is every recurring unit of work expressed as a recurrence rule in the standard grammar, and is that rule the stored source of truth rather than a derived artefact?
questions.evidence_expected: The stored representation of every schedule the platform holds, and whatever the runner actually reads at fire time.
questions.aligned_looks_like: One stored rule per schedule in the standard grammar, and the runner expands that rule; nothing else defines when work happens.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Rules kept in a platform-specific interval syntax, or a standard rule stored for display while a hand-written timer decides the real fire times.

questions.question: The proposed future state turns on deep use, so: are the grammar's distinguishing mechanisms actually exercised - by-day and by-month-day selection, count and until bounds, and exception or override dates - or is every stored rule reducible to a fixed interval?
questions.evidence_expected: The set of distinct rule shapes in use, and one rule that cannot be expressed as a fixed interval, with the fire times it produces.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Rules use positional and calendar selectors and bounded ends; at least one rule in production is inexpressible as a fixed interval.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Every rule is every-N-minutes or every-N-days, so the grammar is a label over what an interval timer would have done.

questions.question: The proposed future state turns on deep use, so: does expansion preserve local wall time across a daylight-saving transition, and are bounded ends interpreted in the absolute frame the standard requires?
questions.evidence_expected: The fire times produced for a daily rule spanning a daylight-saving boundary in a zone that observes one, and the interpretation of a bounded end.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The local time of day is unchanged either side of the transition, the skipped and repeated local times are handled explicitly, and the end bound is evaluated as an absolute instant.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Fire times shift by an hour after the transition, an occurrence is silently lost or duplicated, or the rule was stored without a zone so the question cannot be answered.

questions.question: The guarantee proposed here is applied, not requested, so: when fires are missed because the platform was down, what does the schedule's declared policy say happens, and do the resulting runs carry budget, actor and replay-safety without the schedule's author supplying them?
questions.evidence_expected: A recovery after a deliberate outage spanning several fire times: the runs produced, their keys, their ceilings and their recorded actor.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Catch-up is bounded by a declared lookback and overlap policy, each recovered fire is keyed by schedule and nominal fire time so a repeat converges, and each run carries a ceiling and a named actor nobody passed in.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Every missed fire replays as a storm, or all missed fires are silently dropped, or recovered runs are unattributed and uncapped.

questions.question: Against the proposed future state across every entry, can a schedule be created, paused, edited and backfilled from any of the four entries, and does a fire travel the same downstream path as work arriving from a person, an event or an external system?
questions.evidence_expected: The same schedule operated once from an interactive entry and once by an external caller, plus a trace comparing a scheduled run with an equivalent run started by a person.
questions.aligned_looks_like: One interface for schedule operations regardless of entry, and the two traces differ only in how the work arrived.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Schedules can only be changed by editing host configuration or redeploying, or scheduled fires take a separate code path with different validation, refusal or recording.

questions.question: Against the proposed future state, is rule expansion separated from fire delivery behind an interface, with a second implementation whose durability model differs, so the platform can move between a durable execution service and a plain conforming parser plus timer?
questions.evidence_expected: The interface, both implementations, and one suite of rules whose expected fire times both must produce.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Identical fire times from both; the swap changes only wiring; catch-up and overlap policy are expressed in the interface, not inherited from one runner's features.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Scheduling semantics defined by whatever one runner happens to do, so the contract cannot be stated without naming it.

standard.name: idempotency-key convention
standard.why: The direction is unmistakable but nothing has ratified. The header is an IETF HTTPAPI working-group Internet-Draft at draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header-07, published 15 October 2025 with intended status Standards Track and an expiry of 18 April 2026 - inside the window it lapsed without becoming an RFC, having run since 2021. Meanwhile the payload side is converging on the event envelope identifier as the stable dedup key, while provider conventions - retry windows, conflict codes, key scope - remain fragmented, so the practice is de facto rather than standard. The future state therefore names the mechanism to hold, a durable keyed claim, and the exit if the draft dies: the same claim store keyed off the envelope identifier, with the header treated as one accepted spelling among several.

future_state.text: Every externally triggered unit of work carries a key on the wire in the convention's form, and the platform turns that key into a durable claim rather than a log line: a client-generated key, a database uniqueness constraint that arbitrates the race, a request fingerprint, an explicit in_progress state with a lease, and storing the outcome in the same transaction as the side effect. A replay with the same key and the same fingerprint returns the stored outcome without re-executing; a replay with the same key and a different fingerprint is refused with a typed conflict naming the mismatch rather than silently executing the new payload; a claim whose lease has expired because the holder died is reclaimable by exactly one contender, so a crash mid-run neither wedges the key forever nor permits two executions. Keys are scoped to the operation they protect, are retained for at least the longest retry window any producer is permitted, and where a producer supplies no key the platform derives one from the arriving envelope's own identifier, so replay-safety is a property of the entry rather than a courtesy of the caller. The exit, should the header convention be abandoned, is that only the accepted spelling changes: the claim store, the fingerprint and the lease are the contract.
future_state.quote: a client-generated key, a database uniqueness constraint that arbitrates the race, a request fingerprint, an explicit in_progress state with a lease, and storing the outcome in the same transaction as the side effect

direction.text: Inside the window the header draft stalled - version 07 of October 2025 expired in April 2026 with no RFC - so the convention is settling by practice rather than by ratification, and the practical centre of gravity moved to the durable claim behind the key and to the event envelope identifier as the key when a producer supplies none. Guidance is now explicit that your deduplication cache must persist at least as long as the provider's full retry window, and that check-then-act without a uniqueness constraint, writing the key after the side effect, and skipping the request fingerprint are the three ways an implementation looks correct and is not. What is being abandoned: short-lived in-memory dedup caches, and the assumption that networks can be made to deliver exactly once instead of making processing idempotent. It would be an error now to accept a key and merely record it, to give the key a shorter retention than the longest producer retry window, or to build a bespoke per-producer dedup scheme where the envelope identifier is already stable.
direction.quote: Your deduplication cache must persist at least as long as the provider's full retry window

questions.question: Against the proposed future state, is a key accepted on the wire at every externally triggered entry, and is a request that omits one still made replay-safe?
questions.evidence_expected: The accepted request shape at each entry, and the stored claim produced by a request that carried no key.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The key is accepted in the conventional form everywhere it can arrive, and where absent the platform derives one from the arriving envelope's identifier.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Only one entry accepts a key, or a missing key means the request simply executes with no claim recorded.

questions.question: The proposed future state turns on deep use, so: behind the key, is there a durable claim - a uniqueness constraint that arbitrates the race, a stored request fingerprint, an in-progress lease, and the outcome persisted with the side effect - or is the key only recorded?
questions.evidence_expected: Two identical requests issued concurrently with one key, and the resulting stored claim, outcome and responses.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Exactly one execution; the loser receives the stored outcome or an in-progress signal; the outcome and the claim were committed together.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Both execute; or the loser gets an error with no stored outcome; or the claim is written after the side effect, leaving a crash window that double-executes.

questions.question: The proposed future state turns on deep use, so: what happens when the same key arrives with a different payload, and what happens when the holder of a claim dies mid-execution?
questions.evidence_expected: A replay of one key with an altered payload, and a run killed after claiming a key and before completing, followed by a retry of the same key.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The altered payload is refused as a typed conflict naming the fingerprint mismatch, with no side effect attempted; the abandoned claim is reclaimed by exactly one retry after its lease lapses.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: The altered payload silently returns the earlier result or silently executes the new one; the abandoned claim wedges the key permanently, or two retries both reclaim it.

questions.question: The guarantee proposed here is applied, not requested, so: is claim retention at least as long as the longest retry window of any producer permitted to reach the platform, and is that relationship enforced rather than assumed?
questions.evidence_expected: The retention setting of the claim store, the maximum retry window of each admitted producer, and a replay issued just before retention expires.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Retention is derived from the longest admitted retry window and the late replay still returns the stored outcome without re-executing.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: A fixed short retention chosen for storage cost, so a late redelivery or an operator replay executes as new work.

questions.question: Against the proposed future state across every entry, across a person retrying, an event redelivered, a scheduled fire caught up after an outage, and an external partner retrying a timed-out call, do all four converge on one execution and one answer for the same logical action?
questions.evidence_expected: One logical action driven through all four entries with the corresponding key, and the resulting execution count and returned bodies.
questions.aligned_looks_like: One execution total; every entry returns the same outcome body; the deduplication decision is made in one place, not per entry.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Duplicate executions across entries, different answers for the same key depending on where the retry arrived, or per-entry dedup logic that can disagree.

questions.question: Against the proposed future state, does the keyed claim store sit behind a capability interface, with a second implementation whose concurrency mechanism differs, and does the interface state its atomicity requirement rather than inheriting it?
questions.evidence_expected: The interface, both implementations, and a concurrency suite run against each.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The interface names the atomic claim-or-return operation and its lease semantics; both implementations pass the same race and reclaim tests.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: One store, or a contract whose correctness depends on a feature only the incumbent provides, so the claim cannot be moved.

questions.question: Against the direction proposed for this section, is the key treated as one accepted spelling over a durable claim contract, so that the build survives the header convention failing to ratify?
questions.evidence_expected: The mapping from each accepted key source - the header form, the envelope identifier, a derived key - onto the same claim record.
questions.aligned_looks_like: All sources normalise to one claim; changing or adding a spelling touches only the intake mapping.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: The unratified header form is baked into storage, refusal codes and downstream logic, so abandoning it is a rewrite rather than a mapping change.

standard.name: — (no standard; original design under B5)
standard.why: Part B records no standard for this boundary and points at B5, so the future state is original design held to the five things B5 requires a state contract to specify: the write model, concurrency and single-writer guarantees, the integrity mechanism, retention, and the query surface planning needs. The design is not unconstrained, though: three settled techniques are available to borrow from inside the window rather than invent. RFC 9162 shows that the append-only property of a log is obtained from a Merkle tree that yields inclusion and consistency proofs; commodity object storage now offers conditional writes that behave as compare-and-swap, so single-writer arbitration no longer needs a database; and event-store practice has converged on expected-version optimistic concurrency with projections for reads and snapshot or compaction for retention.

future_state.text: State is one append-only history behind a capability interface, not a file format: a write is an append of an immutable record to a named stream, admitted only if the caller's expected version is still current, so the store arbitrates a single logical writer per stream instead of trusting convention, and a torn or partial record is never visible to a reader. Integrity is stronger than a per-record hash link, because the append-only property of each log is achieved using Merkle Trees: a reader can be given an inclusion proof for one record and a consistency proof that the history it saw yesterday is a prefix of the history today, so an edit, a reorder and a truncation are all detectable, and detectable by an independent verifier that was not written by the platform. Retention is declared per stream, with snapshots or compaction bounding replay cost while the proof structure over the retained history survives, and deletion is itself a recorded, provable event rather than a silent gap. The read surface is stated as operations that cost planning actually needs - a record by identity, a stream from a version, and a materialised projection - so the contract mentions no file, path or layout, and an embedded log, an object store with conditional writes, or a transactional database can each serve behind it unchanged.
future_state.quote: the append-only property of each log is achieved using Merkle Trees

direction.text: Inside the window three things settled that a state design should now assume. First, conditional writes reached commodity object storage - S3 supports conditional writes using If-Match with ETag, and this pattern closely resembles a compare-and-swap (CAS) operation and enables optimistic concurrency control without locks - with nearly every other object store already offering preconditions, so a durable append-only log on plain storage with real single-writer arbitration is now ordinary rather than exotic, and write-ahead logs are being moved into the storage layer on that basis. Second, transparency-log technique (RFC 9162 Merkle inclusion and consistency proofs, already extended to key transparency and module mirrors) is being applied directly to agent audit history in 2026 research. Third, event-store practice has converged on expected-version optimistic concurrency, projections as the read surface, and snapshot or policy-driven compaction for retention. What is being abandoned: single-file, single-process state with no concurrency control, and integrity by chained hash alone with no proof of consistency or truncation. It would be an error now to write a contract in terms of a file layout, or to build a chain only the writer's own code can verify by re-reading the whole history.
direction.quote: This pattern closely resembles a compare-and-swap (CAS) operation and enables optimistic concurrency control without locks

questions.question: Against the proposed future state, is there a written state contract that specifies all five of the write model, concurrency and single-writer guarantees, the integrity mechanism, retention, and the query surface - stated without reference to any storage format?
questions.evidence_expected: The contract document or interface definition, with each of the five located in it.
questions.aligned_looks_like: All five specified, each with a checkable criterion, and no file, path or serialisation appears in the contract.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Fewer than five specified, or the contract is the description of a file format, so replacing the storage means renegotiating the contract.

questions.question: The proposed future state turns on deep use, so: can an independent verifier prove that a given record is in the history and that an earlier history is a prefix of the current one, and does that verification detect a truncation of the most recent records?
questions.evidence_expected: A verification run by a tool the platform did not write, over a history that has been edited in the middle, and over one whose tail has been removed.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Both tampering forms are detected, and the proof needed to detect them is small rather than requiring the whole history to be re-read.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Only a mid-history edit is caught while truncation passes, or verification requires the platform's own code and full replay, so no outside party can check it.

questions.question: The proposed future state turns on deep use, so: how is a concurrent write to the same stream arbitrated, and what does a reader see if the writer dies mid-append?
questions.evidence_expected: Two writers appending to one stream at the same expected version, and a write interrupted by killing the process, followed by a read.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The store rejects the stale write on an expected-version or conditional check and the loser retries; the interrupted append is either fully present or fully absent.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Both writes land and one is lost or the history forks; or a partial record is readable; or single-writer holds only because one process happens to be running.

questions.question: Against the proposed future state, are there two implementations with genuinely different durability models behind one interface, passing one conformance suite, and does the core import only the interface?
questions.evidence_expected: The suite output for both, and the change set that swapped them.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Both pass identical concurrency, integrity and query tests; the swap touches wiring only; no component reaches past the interface to the underlying store.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: One implementation, or a second of the same shape, or components that read the underlying storage directly for convenience.

questions.question: Against the proposed future state across every entry, do units of work arriving from all four entries write through the same append path, and can cost planning answer its questions from the stated read operations without scanning the whole history?
questions.evidence_expected: The write path taken from each entry, and the reads a planning pass issues for a realistic history, with their cost.
questions.aligned_looks_like: One append path for every entry; planning is served by record-by-identity, stream-from-version and projection reads whose cost does not grow with total history.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Some entry writes by a side path, or every planning pass replays the entire history because the read surface was never specified.

questions.question: Against the direction proposed for this section, is retention a declared, enforced policy per stream that keeps verification possible over what remains, or is history kept forever by default and pruned by hand when it hurts?
questions.evidence_expected: The retention policy per stream, a snapshot or compaction run, and a verification over the history after that run.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Retention declared with the unit of work it belongs to; compaction or snapshotting bounds replay cost; verification still succeeds afterwards and the removal is itself recorded.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: No retention policy, or pruning that breaks verification or leaves an unexplained gap, so the integrity claim quietly stops holding as the history grows.

gaps.claim: That inclusion and consistency proofs are practical at the write rate a busy agent platform generates, rather than at certificate-issuance rates.
gaps.research_query: transparency log throughput write rate benchmark 2026 merkle inclusion proof high volume application log

gaps.claim: That a single read surface of record-by-identity, stream-from-version and projection is sufficient for cost planning over a typed dependency structure - this is my synthesis, not a sourced finding.
gaps.research_query: event sourced graph query surface projections planning cost estimation read model design 2026

standard.name: — (no standard recorded; a platform-applied guarantee)
standard.why: Part B records no standard for this concern, and none has settled, but the direction became visible inside the window: run-scoped, in-session enforcement moved from advice to shipped primitive, with two major agent platforms shipping run-level spend enforcement a day apart at different layers - one in the session object, one at the gateway - and practitioner guidance converging on a guard that checks cumulative spend before each call and terminates the session at the ceiling, backed by a second enforcement layer the agent's own code cannot bypass. The measurement substrate is still pre-stable: the GenAI semantic conventions that carry gen_ai.usage.input_tokens and gen_ai.usage.output_tokens remained in Development status as of May 2026 with no stabilisation timeline. The exit, should the accounting attributes change, is that the ceiling and its enforcement points are the contract and the unit of measure is a mapping.

future_state.text: Every unit of work is admitted with a ceiling attached by the platform before execution, derived from an estimate produced by pure planning and compared against a policy limit, so refusal happens before spend rather than being discovered afterwards; the ceiling is expressed in units the platform actually measures - tokens, currency, wall time, tool invocations - and is carried on the unit, not held in an account-level cap. Enforcement is continuous rather than periodic: code that checks cumulative token or cost spend before each API call and terminates the agent session when a defined ceiling is hit, with a second checkpoint at the capability boundary so the code inside the unit cannot bypass it, and with sub-units drawing from the parent's remaining ceiling rather than each receiving a fresh one, because multi-agent spend compounds rather than adding. Exhaustion terminates that unit and only that unit: siblings and the platform continue, any partial result is retained and recorded, and the caller receives a typed refusal naming the ceiling, the consumption and the unit - never a truncated success. A resumed, retried or replayed unit continues under the ceiling it had left, and the consumption of every unit is recorded against the same attributes telemetry uses, so the ceiling and the accounting cannot drift apart. The exit, if the accounting attributes are renamed or stabilise differently, is a mapping at the recording boundary rather than a change to where ceilings are enforced.
future_state.quote: code that checks cumulative token or cost spend before each API call and terminates the agent session when a defined ceiling is hit

direction.text: Inside the window budget control moved from reporting to enforcement. The framing that settled is blunt: the only reliable cost control mechanism is one that enforces a ceiling during the session - not one that estimates costs upfront and hopes; run-scoped enforcement shipped in two major agent platforms a day apart, Anthropic in the session object and AWS at the gateway, which shows the layer is still being chosen while the requirement is not. Alongside it, pre-execution admission is established practice in infrastructure automation - the agent proposes, the estimate is computed, the policy rejects, and nothing is created - and practitioners now describe three layers, a pre-run cost check that can reject, a platform quota, and a hard account backstop, of which only the first two prevent spend rather than reporting it. Token accounting has a standard vocabulary in the OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions but those remain in Development status as of May 2026. What is being abandoned: monthly account caps as the only guard, and per-call limits that do nothing about a loop. It would be an error now to make the budget advisory, to check it only between top-level steps, or to give each spawned sub-agent a fresh ceiling, since sub-agent context feeds back into the orchestrator and compounds.
direction.quote: The only reliable cost control mechanism is one that enforces a ceiling during the session - not one that estimates costs upfront and hopes

questions.question: Against the proposed future state, does every unit of work carry a ceiling, including ones whose caller never mentioned a budget, and can the platform name that ceiling for any unit currently running?
questions.evidence_expected: The set of in-flight units with the ceiling attached to each, and a unit started by a request that carried no budget field.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Every unit has a ceiling; where the caller supplied none the platform attached one from policy at admission.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Ceilings exist only where a caller passed one, or exist as a global account limit that cannot be attributed to a unit.

questions.question: The proposed future state turns on deep use, so: is the ceiling checked before each spending call within a unit, and does a sub-unit draw from its parent's remaining ceiling rather than receiving its own?
questions.evidence_expected: A run deliberately driven past its ceiling in a tight loop, with the point of termination, and a run that spawns sub-units, with the consumption accounted at each level.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Termination lands at the ceiling with at most one call of overshoot; parent and children share one remaining balance that decreases monotonically.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: The check happens only between top-level steps so a loop overshoots by a wide margin, or each sub-unit starts fresh so total spend is a multiple of the stated ceiling.

questions.question: The guarantee proposed here is applied, not requested, so: can the code inside a unit exceed, raise or disable its own ceiling, and is there an enforcement point outside that code?
questions.evidence_expected: An attempt from inside a unit to raise its own ceiling or to call a capability directly, and the result.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The attempt is refused; a second checkpoint at the capability boundary stops the spend even when in-unit accounting is wrong or bypassed.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: The budget is a parameter the unit passes to itself, or the only check lives in the same code path the unit controls, so a bug or a prompt injection removes it.

questions.question: The proposed future state turns on deep use, so: when a ceiling is exhausted, what exactly stops, what survives, and what does the record say?
questions.evidence_expected: The state of the platform, sibling units and the exhausted unit's partial output immediately after an exhaustion, plus the recorded outcome.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Only that unit terminates; siblings and the platform continue; partial results are retained and marked as partial; the outcome records the ceiling, the consumption and the point of termination.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: The process or the whole run dies with it, or the unit continues while merely flagged, or the outcome is indistinguishable from an ordinary failure or a success.

questions.question: Against the proposed future state across every entry, for each of the four entries, where does the ceiling come from and what does the caller see when it is hit - including the schedule and event entries, where nobody is present to be asked?
questions.evidence_expected: One unit exhausted at each entry, with the origin of its ceiling and the body returned or recorded at that entry.
questions.aligned_looks_like: Every entry attaches a ceiling from policy without asking, and each returns or records the same typed refusal naming ceiling and consumption; non-interactive entries inherit the ceiling of the schedule or subscription owner.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: Only the interactive entry enforces, or non-interactive fires run uncapped, or the same exhaustion is reported differently at different entries.

questions.question: Against the direction proposed for this section, is cost knowable before commitment - does an estimate exist before execution begins, get compared to the ceiling, and cause a refusal with nothing spent?
questions.evidence_expected: A unit whose estimate exceeds its ceiling, with the estimate, the refusal and the measured spend for that attempt.
questions.aligned_looks_like: The estimate is produced by planning alone, the refusal precedes any execution, spend for the refused attempt is zero, and estimate versus actual is recorded for later comparison.
questions.misaligned_looks_like: No estimate exists, or the estimate is produced by starting the work, or refusal happens after spend so the cap only reports what already happened.
